congenial: Congenial describes someone pleasant and easy to get along with. It can also mean that something suits a person or situation well. It emphasizes a good fit rather than simple politeness.
conjugal: Conjugal describes things connected with marriage or the partnership between married partners. It sounds formal and old-fashioned, so you often see it in law, religion, or official writing. It is close to marital, but focuses on the marriage itself.
connect-the-dots: See how separate facts fit together and understand the bigger story. People use it when evidence or observations start to show a clear pattern. It is similar to putting pieces together until the full answer becomes clear.
connoisseur: A connoisseur is someone who knows a subject deeply and can judge its quality. People use it for art, food, wine, or cars, where it suggests informed taste rather than simple enjoyment.
connubial: Connubial describes something connected with marriage or the relationship between spouses. It sounds formal and slightly old-fashioned, and often appears in legal, historical, or ceremonial writing. It is similar to conjugal, but is more literary.
conscientious: A conscientious person works carefully, acts responsibly, and tries to do the right thing. They usually keep this steady behavior over time. It is a strong compliment, similar to saying someone is careful and dependable.
consensus: Consensus is a decision that most of the group can agree on and live with. It does not always mean everyone feels strongly positive about it. A leader may ask for consensus before moving forward, although seeking it can take more time.
consider-it-done: You are saying that the task is finished and needs no more work. It sounds clear, confident, and final, so use it when you can honestly promise completion. In sensitive situations, a warmer explanation may sound better.
consternation: Consternation is the shock and worry you feel when something sudden and alarming happens. It is stronger and more formal than simple concern, and it often includes fear or dismay. You might hear it in news reports or serious accounts of a difficult event.
constrict: To constrict something is to make it narrower, tighter or more limited. The word can describe a physical object or a person’s choices and freedom. It is similar to restrict, but often suggests pressure or squeezing.
construe: To construe something is to understand or interpret it in a particular way. The word can sound careful and analytical, but it may also suggest that the interpretation is unusual or difficult to accept.
contemptuous: Being contemptuous shows that you think someone or something deserves very little respect. It describes words, actions, or an attitude that clearly signals dislike and disregard. It is stronger than dismissive, which can simply mean showing little interest.
contentious: Likely to cause strong disagreement or argument. It can describe a disputed subject, a difficult meeting, or a person who often argues. It is stronger than controversial, which means people hold different views.
contort: To contort something is to twist or bend it until it has an unnatural shape. People use the word for bodies, faces, and writing that feels twisted or forced. It is similar to distort, but contort focuses more on the twisting shape.
contrite: Feeling contrite means being deeply sorry for what you have done and ready to accept responsibility. It is stronger than a quick apology and suggests real regret, not just politeness. The word is formal and often used in serious conversations or official statements.
controversial: A controversial person, idea, or decision causes strong disagreement or criticism. People often use it for politics, laws, creative work, and public actions. It means the subject is disputed, not necessarily that it is wrong.
cool-calm-and-collected: Someone stays relaxed, emotionally steady, and able to think clearly during a difficult moment. People use it when a person handles pressure with confidence, rather than simply saying that the situation feels calm.
cope: Dealing with a hard situation and still being able to continue is coping. People often use cope with for problems, stress, or painful feelings, and it does not mean the problem has gone away. It can sound more serious than manage, which can suggest keeping control of a task.
copious: Copious means there is a large amount of something, often more than is needed. People may describe food, plants, details or evidence this way. It sounds formal and can sometimes suggest an excessive quantity.
cordial: A cordial manner is warm, polite, and friendly without being too familiar. You often hear it used for formal greetings, welcomes, or friendly relations between groups. It is not the same as emotional; cordial describes how someone acts, even when they do not know the other person well.
corpulent: A large or overweight body is what this describes. It is a formal, often blunt word, so use it carefully when talking about a person. Overweight is more common in everyday English.
corroborate: New facts or another source can support an account and make it stronger. Corroborate is a formal word often used in reports and investigations, while confirm is more common in everyday speech.
cost-an-arm-and-a-leg: Something is far more expensive than you expected. The image of paying with an arm and a leg makes the cost feel extreme, but the phrase is usually light and casual.
coterie: A coterie is a small, close group of people who share an interest, background, or social connection. The word may sound approving, but it can also suggest that the group is exclusive or snobbish. It is similar to clique.
could-hear-a-pin-drop: The place is so quiet that even a small pin falling would be easy to hear. People use it to show how silent a room or group is, often because everyone is listening or waiting for someone to speak.
coup: A sudden move that gives someone power or a big advantage. In political news, it usually means a quick takeover of government. In casual English, it can also mean an impressive success, but that use is quite old.
cover-ones-bases: You prepare for several possible problems so that none can catch you by surprise. It might mean checking different prices, keeping spare parts, or asking about both plans. It comes from baseball, where players touch every base to protect their position.
covert: Secret activity that is deliberately hidden from others is covert. It can describe behaviour, actions or a hidden purpose, and it often carries a suspicious feeling. Clandestine is a closely related word.
covet: To covet something is to want it very strongly because it belongs to someone else or is not available to you. The word often suggests greed and is more negative than just want. Covet is commonly confused with crave, but it puts another person's possession at the center.
crack-down: Take stronger action against rule-breaking or other problems. It means using firmer rules, more checks, or greater pressure to stop bad behavior. It is often used when managers or authorities respond to repeated problems.
crave: A strong desire that is hard to ignore or control is a craving, and to crave is to feel it. People crave food, attention, or a particular outcome. Unlike covet, crave does not require the thing to belong to someone else, though the desire can be just as strong.
credit-where-credits-due: People should be recognized for the work they did. You say this when someone was missed or did not get enough credit. It may sound sincere, but it can also be a firm reminder that their contribution matters.
credulous: Someone who believes claims too easily is credulous. This word criticizes their judgement and suggests they have not checked the facts. It sounds stronger and more negative than gullible.
criterion: A criterion is a standard used to judge whether something is good, successful, or acceptable. People use it in careful discussion when they want a precise rule or measure for making a decision.
cross-my-heart: You promise that what you are saying is completely true. The image comes from making a cross over your heart as a serious sign of a promise. It adds warmth and strong feeling, but can sound playful or overly dramatic.
cry-foul: Crying foul means complaining strongly that someone has acted unfairly or broken the rules. It can describe a real complaint, but it may also suggest that the complaint is too loud. People often use it when one side wants others to notice an alleged injustice.
cry-ones-eyes-out: Cry your eyes out means crying a very large amount. People use it for deep sadness, grief, or strong relief. It is often more dramatic than simply saying you cried, but it can describe real tears too.
cry-wolf: You raise a warning that nobody believes, because you have cried about it before. After that, a real problem can arrive and be ignored too. The story behind it is a boy who shouted that a wolf was coming, until people stopped coming to help him.
cryptic: A cryptic message has a hidden meaning or is written in a confusing way. It may be deliberately mysterious, as in a puzzle, or simply hard to understand. People often use it with clues or messages.
culminate: Culminate means to reach the final point or result after some time and effort. It is often used for a project or series of events that build toward a major outcome. The word sounds polished and formal.
culpable: Someone who deserves blame for a harmful act is culpable. This is a strong, formal word often used in legal and workplace settings. It is more serious than simply being at fault.
culprit: A culprit is the person responsible for something wrong or harmful. In less formal speech, it can also mean the main cause of a problem. It is often used when identifying someone who caused trouble.
cumbersome: Something cumbersome is difficult to carry, handle or use because it is heavy, large or complicated. It can describe luggage, systems or procedures. The word stresses inconvenience rather than making something completely impossible.
cumulative: A cumulative effect grows as separate amounts or changes are added together. It is often used with losses, gains, impacts and results. The key idea is that many small parts create one growing total.
cup-of-tea: Something can be your cup of tea when you enjoy it and find it pleasant. People often use it with not to say that something is not right for their taste. It is common in British and Irish English, but now many people understand it elsewhere.
cupidity: Cupidity is a strong wish for money, property, or other valuable things. It sounds formal and critical, and often describes greed in a moral or historical way. Cupidity is not simply the same as envy: it focuses on possessing valuable things, often because of what they give you.
cursory: When you do something in a hurry, without really looking at the details. People use it when a check was quick and maybe too quick. Do not confuse it with careful, which means the opposite.
curtail: To curtail an activity is to stop it early or make it shorter than planned. People use it for trips, spending, talks and projects. It sounds more formal than cut short, while suggesting a deliberate reduction.
cut-a-dash: Someone cuts a dash when they behave in a lively, stylish, or showy way that gets attention. The literal picture is a person making a quick, striking movement through the air. It is usually light and admiring, but it can also have a joking tone.
cut-a-deal: To discuss the terms and finally agree on an arrangement. It often involves money, work, or responsibilities, and the two sides may each give up something. It is common in business and negotiations.
cut-a-wide-swath: Cutting a wide swath means having a strong effect on many people or on a whole area of work. The image comes from cutting a broad path through tall grass, leaving a large clear space behind. It suggests wide impact, not just a small change.
cut-both-ways: A choice or action can help in one way but cause harm in another. The picture is a blade that cuts in two directions. People use it when the same thing has both good and bad results, such as a useful change that also costs money.
cut-corners: To save time or money by leaving out important steps. It is usually critical because the result may be careless or unsafe. The picture is taking a short diagonal path around a corner.
cut-ones-teeth: Gain practical experience, especially early in your career. It suggests learning through real challenges and hard work, not only through lessons or study. People often use it to praise someone’s growth and preparation.
cut-red-tape: Remove unnecessary rules, steps, or paperwork so a process becomes easier. It is common in workplaces when people want to make a system faster and simpler. The image is cutting through red tape tied around official documents.
cut-someone-some-slack: Being less strict or critical than usual, especially when someone has made a mistake or had a hard time. It comes from giving someone extra rope so they have more room to move; people often say this after a mistake has already happened.
cynic: A cynic doubts that people are honest or will act well. They may expect selfish or disappointing behavior from others. The word can sound a little harsh, but it often describes distrust of people’s motives.
cynical: Being cynical means expecting people to act mainly for their own benefit or to behave dishonestly. It can show sharp distrust or tired disappointment, so it may sound negative if used often. Skeptical asks if a claim is true; cynical often assumes bad motives behind it.
daily-grind: The daily grind is the same dull or tiring tasks that fill your normal routine. It often means work, study, or household jobs that keep coming back. People use it to describe the boring side of everyday life.
dark-horse: A dark horse is a person or thing that wins or succeeds when few people expected it to. The image is a little-known racehorse beating stronger rivals. It often means someone was underestimated before becoming successful.
dauntless: Someone dauntless keeps going even when something is frightening or difficult. It shows steady courage, not a careless lack of fear. People often use it for heroic actions, so it can sound slightly formal.
day-in-day-out: Something happens day in, day out when it is part of your normal routine and keeps happening again and again. The picture of one day following another shows that it never stops. It can feel neutral, but it often suggests that the repetition is tiring.
daylight-robbery: A theft done openly in broad daylight, often with force or threats. People also use it for an outrageous price, like a hotel charging a lot for basic food. It is more dramatic than the simple word theft because the victim had no chance to escape.
dead-end: A dead end is a situation where you cannot continue or move forward. It may describe a failed plan, a road that ends, or a job with little chance to progress. Unlike a break, it suggests there is no useful way ahead.
dead-giveaway: An obvious sign that reveals what someone meant to hide. It often means they showed the secret by accident, like blushing when they claim not to be nervous. People also use it for any clue that makes a conclusion easy.
dead-heat: Two or more competitors finish together, with the same score or level. It is common in sport, racing and business, and it tells you the result was very close. People sometimes also use it to mean a tie for first place.
dead-on: A guess or judgment is dead-on when it is completely correct and hits the exact point. The picture is an arrow landing directly on a target, with no error. In another context, it can also mean arriving at exactly the right time.
dearth: A dearth means there is not enough of something people need or value. It often suggests a serious shortage that creates difficulty. The word is mainly used in formal writing, especially about food, workers, housing or opportunities.
death-and-taxes: Death and taxes are presented as two things that everyone must eventually face and pay for. The phrase jokingly names them as facts of life that cannot be avoided. People often use it when talking about unavoidable costs or responsibilities.
death-by-a-thousand-paper-cuts: Be worn down slowly by many small problems. Each issue may seem minor, but together they become tiring and hard to deal with. The phrase can be serious or slightly funny, depending on the situation.
debacle: A debacle is a sudden, total failure that causes confusion or disorder. It is much stronger and more dramatic than saying a plan failed. Use it for a serious mess, not a small mistake or setback.
debilitate: To make someone or something weaker is the basic idea. It can describe lost health, less power, or a reduced ability to act. It sounds serious and formal, especially in reports.
debris: Broken pieces left behind after something is damaged make up debris. It often means a mass of stone, wood, glass, or similar material, not one whole object. You might find it after an earthquake or explosion.
decade: A decade is a period of ten years. People use it for a particular time marked by an important change, such as the decade of rapid growth. It can also simply mean any ten years, so do not confuse it with a century.
decadence: Decadence is excessive luxury, pleasure, or self-indulgence, often linked to a society losing its values. The word is usually critical, so it is stronger and more moral than simply enjoying something. Decadence often goes with decline, decay, and wealth.
decapitate: To cut off someone’s head. Figuratively, it means to remove the most important part of something and destroy its value. It is a blunt, disturbing word, so it suits forceful writing more than daily speech.
decisive: Someone decisive knows what they want and chooses fast. We also say a decision was decisive when it settled a matter. It can sound negative if a person is too bossy and decides everything alone.
declaim: To declaim means to speak loudly and with strong feeling, often as if performing for others. It can also mean to state something boldly without careful proof. It sounds more dramatic than simply speak.
decorum: Decorum means behaving with dignity, politeness, and care for what suits the situation. People use it for formal events, sensitive meetings, or proper conduct in public. It sounds old-fashioned and is close to respectability.
decrepit: Something decrepit is so old, weak or damaged that it seems barely able to work. People may call an old building, machine or vehicle decrepit. It is stronger and more dramatic than simply old or worn out.
deem: To think that something is a certain way, in an official and confident tone. You meet it in legal or school writing, like they deemed the case closed. It is more formal than consider, which is the everyday word.
deep-dive: Look at a subject carefully and in detail. It means spending time and effort to understand a topic, find useful facts, or solve a problem. The image of going deep below the water shows close attention to what is hidden.
deep-down: Deep down means in your real innermost feelings, below what others may see. You use it to show what you truly think, believe, or care about most. It can sometimes reveal a truth that your normal behavior hides.
defamatory: Statements that unfairly damage someone’s reputation are defamatory. This serious word is common in legal disputes and public condemnations. It usually points to false claims that can harm a person’s standing.
deference: Deference is polite respect, especially when you accept someone’s authority, wishes, or opinion. It can show admiration, but it may also suggest giving too much power to another person. It is more than simple respect.
deft: Deft means skilled and quick, especially when using your hands. The action looks smooth and easy, rather than clumsy or forced. It can also describe a clever and precise performance.
degrade: To degrade something is to make its quality, value, or condition worse. It can describe damage over time or an action that lowers something’s status. It often has a critical tone and is stronger than simply making something poorer.
delegate: Giving someone else part of your work or responsibility is to delegate. It can show trust and good management. If you only pass on the boring parts, people may think you are dumping work on them.
deleterious: Damage or harm to people, places, or results is what this word points to. It sounds serious and formal, and people often use it in medicine, science, law, or news about harmful policies.
deliberate: If you did something on purpose, it was deliberate. As an adjective it can also mean slow and careful, like a deliberate pace. As a verb it means thinking carefully before you decide.
delineation: A clear outline that shows where one thing ends and another begins. You find it in school books and legal papers where differences are marked carefully. In daily talk, simply say description or explanation.
delude: To delude someone is to make them believe something false or misleading. It often refers to false hopes or appearances that deceive people. Delude oneself is a common phrase for holding a mistaken belief.
delve: To look into something carefully, like a detective reading the fine print. People use it for research and for understanding hard ideas. It sounds more serious than the everyday look into.
demeanor: Your demeanor is the way you look and behave in front of others. A calm or friendly demeanor can give a first impression before you speak. It focuses on outward conduct, unlike character, which means deeper qualities.
demur: To demur means to pause or raise a small objection, especially in a formal situation. As a noun, it means that hesitation or objection. It sounds polite and old-fashioned, rather than a strong refusal.
denigrated: When someone or something is denigrated, it is attacked with harsh and often unfair criticism. People use this formal word in writing about a person’s character, work, or reputation.
denote: To denote means to act as a sign or label for a particular meaning. This is common in formal and academic writing. It is close to signify, but it focuses more on the direct meaning.
denouement: The ending of a story where the mystery is finally solved. It comes after lots of questions and tension. In real life you can also call the final answer of a hard situation its denouement.
depict: To depict means to show or describe someone or something through words, pictures, or charts. It often appears in formal writing about art, stories, or study results. It is more careful than simply draw or show.
deplorable: A deplorable action or situation is so bad that it deserves strong disapproval. It sounds formal and emotional, so it can feel too dramatic when describing a small problem.
deploy: To deploy is to put people, tools or resources where they can do useful work. It often suggests a planned action, such as sending a team or using new technology. The word can sound military, but businesses commonly use it for practical actions.
deprecate: To deprecate something is to state clearly that you do not approve of it. It can also mean to advise against something old or no longer recommended, so it may go with advice.
deride: To deride someone or something is to mock it with clear contempt. It is stronger than disagree and can sound hostile, although it may also describe light teasing.
derived: Coming from something else, like numbers you get from a formula. We use it for facts, results and figures that come from other information. It often goes with from, as in derived from.
derogatory: Derogatory words or actions show contempt or disrespect toward someone. People often use this word for comments, labels, or treatment; it is more formal than simply negative.
desist: This asks someone to stop an action that has continued for a while. It can sound firm or impatient, especially in the form desist from doing something. People often use it in official notices or when they want a clear boundary.
despot: A despot is a ruler with total power who does not allow limits or opposition. The word is very negative and is often used in history and politics. It is similar to dictator, but it puts more focus on power without limits.
destitution: Destitution means having so little money or support that you cannot meet basic needs such as food, housing, and clothing. It is a serious word for extreme poverty and often appears in legal or news reports. People usually say poverty in daily life.
desultory: Moving from one thing to another with no clear plan. It describes talk, reading or work that wanders from topic to topic. People often use it to criticise a conversation that goes nowhere.
deter: Deter means to make someone choose not to do something. A warning, threat, or difficult result may deter them. It is stronger than advise, because it says there is a real reason to stop.
determined: A determined person has a clear goal and keeps trying, even when things go wrong. Their strong intention helps them push through difficulty. It is similar to persistent, but does not necessarily mean stubborn.
detriment: A detriment is harm or a serious disadvantage caused by something. It is often used for effects on health, money, reputation, or future chances. The everyday word harm is simpler, while detriment sounds more formal.
devils-advocate: Someone plays the devil's advocate when they argue the opposite side on purpose. The aim is to test an idea, find weaknesses, or push a group to think more carefully. It does not usually mean they truly disagree; it is often used before a decision.
devout: Devout describes a deep and sincere commitment to a faith, practice, cause, or person. It suggests more than a casual interest and can sound slightly formal. Devout often goes with religious words such as Muslim, Christian, or believer.
dexterity: Moving or handling things quickly and with skill shows dexterity. It can also mean doing a difficult task with sharp control. It is often confused with speed, but control is the key part.
dial-back: Reduce how strong, intense, or demanding something is. It can describe slowing down a plan, lowering pressure, or asking someone to speak more calmly. The image is turning a control to a lower setting.
dial-down: To dial down something is to make it less strong, noisy, demanding, or detailed. The picture comes from turning a control to a lower setting. You might dial down pressure, effort, volume, or conflict without stopping it completely.
diatribe: A diatribe is a long, angry complaint that attacks people or ideas. People use it when a critic seems too harsh and emotional rather than calm. It can sound dismissive at work, so use it for a strong, unfair attack.
didactic: Something didactic is meant to teach a lesson. It can be helpful, but it often feels too serious or preachy, as if the writer wants to tell you what to think. It is often used when teaching feels too direct or full of moral lessons.
die-hard: A die-hard keeps fighting or refuses to change even when giving up seems better. It describes very strong determination, and it can be approving or critical depending on the situation. The image is someone still resisting while they appear to be losing.
die-out: When a practice, animal, tradition, or trend dies out, it becomes less common and then disappears completely. The fading happens gradually rather than stopping all at once. People often use this word when talking about old customs or species becoming lost.
diffident: Diffident people lack confidence, especially when meeting others or taking action. They may hesitate because they are afraid of saying the wrong thing. It is close to shy, but it also suggests uncertainty about how others will react.
dig-deep: Making a much bigger effort or using more of your time, money, or skills. You do this when the usual effort is not enough to reach a difficult goal. The picture is digging far into the ground to find something.
dilatory: Someone who is dilatory is slow to act, especially when a task should be done now. It criticises needless delay, often in work, business, or legal situations. It is close to sluggish, but more formal.
dilettante: A dilettante enjoys an activity but does not take it seriously as a professional. This may simply mean an enthusiastic amateur, but it can also suggest limited skill or commitment. People often call someone a dilettante when they do the activity mainly for fun.
diligent: A diligent person works carefully and keeps making a steady effort. You use it when someone takes their responsibilities seriously and does not give up easily. It describes hard work, not special talent.
diminishing-returns: Getting less extra benefit after putting in more time, money, or effort. For example, studying for many more hours may improve results only a little. It often suggests that you should stop, change direction, or try a better method.
diminutive: A diminutive thing is very small in size, scale or importance. It can also sound cute or endearing, especially for a small child or animal. When used about a person’s role, it may sound slightly insulting.
diplomatic: A diplomatic person chooses words and actions carefully to avoid problems. They may be tactful without hiding the real issue. It also describes official relations between countries, so it is often confused with politics.
discern: To notice or understand something that is not easy to see. You might discern a difference between two voices, or discern that a problem is serious. It suggests careful attention, more than simply seeing.
discerning: Someone discerning notices small differences and understands what matters. People use it as praise for good judgment, and it can describe an eye that sees clear details. It is not the same as knowledgeable, which only means knowing facts.
disciple: A disciple follows and learns from a teacher, leader, or belief. The word suggests commitment and often a strong personal connection, not just a casual interest. It is more common in religious or historical contexts.
discreet: Being discreet means being careful not to share private information or draw attention to yourself. People use it for sensitive matters, but it can also mean small and hard to notice. Do not confuse it with discrete, which means separate and distinct.
disgruntled: Feeling unhappy and dissatisfied because you have been treated badly or ignored makes you disgruntled. The word often carries some bitterness, not just mild sadness. It is stronger than disappointed, which may only mean an expectation was not met.
disheveled: A disheveled person looks untidy, with messy hair or clothes. The word suggests they have been busy, hurried, or too tired to tidy up. It is more noticeable than the basic word messy and is usually informal.
dismantle: Taking something apart means separating its parts, either physically or by examining each part closely. People use it for machines, plans, or systems. Unlike destroy, it suggests careful work rather than sudden damage.
disparage: To disparage someone or something is to describe it in a way that makes it seem less important or valuable. It suggests harsh criticism, not just mild dislike.
disparate: Disparate things are clearly different in type, nature, or quality. People use it for groups, items, or experiences that do not belong together. It is more formal than different and stresses the size of the differences.
dispersed: People or things are dispersed when they are spread over a wide area instead of staying together. The word is often neutral, but it can also suggest that a group has been separated more than people wanted.
disseminate: To disseminate information is to spread it to many people. This is common in official, work, and research settings for news, advice, or study results. It can also mean spreading false claims, so it does not always sound positive.
dissident: A dissident is someone who openly disagrees with a government, organisation, or accepted view. The word suggests courage or strong principles, not just a small argument. It is common in political and social discussions.
distraught: Being so upset, worried, or confused that you cannot think or act normally is being distraught. It is much stronger than simply being distracted or forgetful. People use it for serious emotional strain, so it can sound dramatic in a minor situation.
divergent: Divergent thoughts, results, or paths move in different directions. The word sounds neutral in careful discussion, but it can feel negative when a group is splitting apart. It is not the same as diverse, which simply means varied.
diversity: Diversity means having people with different backgrounds, experiences, identities, or opinions within a group. It is often used positively for teams, schools, and communities. It describes variety, but it does not always mean everyone is treated equally.
divulge: To divulge information is to reveal something that was meant to stay private. It sounds formal and can suggest that the person should not have released it. It is often confused with share, which has no negative feeling.
do-me-a-favour: Do me a favour asks someone to help you, usually in a friendly but direct way. It may also suggest that you will return the help later. At work, could you help me sounds more neutral and professional.
do-or-die: Do or die means making an all-out effort because success matters and there seems to be no safer choice. It shows urgency and strong determination. The words give the simple picture: act and succeed, or fail completely.
dogmatic: A dogmatic person is completely certain about a belief and ignores facts that may prove it wrong. People often use it as criticism because it suggests stubborn, rigid thinking. It can also describe a strict approach to rules.
doleful: Very sad, often in a way that seems a little too dramatic or old-fashioned. It can describe real sorrow, but it may sound slightly comic. It is often confused with mournful, which can sound more serious.
dolorous: Showing deep sadness or grief. It sounds formal and is often used in poetry, music reviews, or serious descriptions of sorrow. It is stronger and less playful than doleful.
domicile: A domicile is the place someone officially counts as home, usually on forms and legal papers. It may differ from where they spend most of their time. In everyday talk, home or address is more natural.
dont-do-anything-i-wouldnt-do: You are telling someone not to take a foolish risk or do something careless. The tone can be caring between friends, but it may sound critical if the speaker has authority. The idea is simple: do not choose what I would avoid.
dont-get-me-wrong: People use this when they want to make sure others understand their real point. It often follows an opinion that may have sounded wrong. It can sound defensive, so explain your meaning right away.
dont-knock-it-till-youve-tried-it: Try or use something before you criticise it. The idea comes from knocking, which means criticising. People often use it to defend a new place, activity, or choice.
dont-knock-it-until-youve-tried-it: Before you criticize or reject something, give it a fair try. The image of knocking on a door suggests checking what is inside before judging it. It is friendly advice, but can sound defensive if you use it during an argument.
dont-mention-it: This is a warm way to tell someone there is no need to say thanks or sorry. It often follows thanks or an apology. It can also gently mean that you will not hold a small problem against someone.
dont-quote-me: Ask someone not to repeat your words. It is often playful among friends, but it can be firm when the words are private or not sure. It is not the same as asking them to keep it a complete secret.
dont-sweat-it: Do not worry because the problem is not serious enough to need your attention. This is a friendly, informal way to reassure someone. It may sound careless if the person truly needs help or the problem is serious.
dont-tell-me: This can show surprise, disbelief, or frustration about an unexpected result. It can also mean you understand, depending on the tone. People sometimes say it playfully to invite someone to continue.
dont-throw-the-baby-out-with-the-bathwat: You should not reject all of something because one part is bad. The literal image is throwing a baby away with the dirty bathwater. It helps you keep the useful part and is a friendly way to warn against an overreaction.
dont-tread-on-me: This is a warning to stay away and not push or cause trouble. The literal image is a dangerous snake under your foot. It can sound strong and rebellious, especially outside a political or historical context.
dont-worry: The situation is likely to be handled or turn out well, so there is no need to feel concerned. People use it to comfort or reassure someone. It can sound too vague if the person is asking for advice or a solution.
dormant: Something dormant is not active now, but it can become active later. This may describe a plan, resource, animal, or hidden ability. It is different from gone, because the possibility still remains.
down-cold: You know or understand something completely, including all the important parts. People use it in informal speech to show that they have mastered a subject or skill. It is stronger than simply knowing something.
down-home: This describes someone who is warm, simple, and not trying to seem special. People use it to show they like a person’s honest manner, but it can also suggest that the person is not very sophisticated. It works best in informal talk.
down-on-ones-knees: Down on one's knees means begging someone very strongly, as if you would kneel to get them to agree. It can show desperation, deep thanks, or a big personal problem. People often use it playfully to make the request feel more serious than it is.
down-the-drain: Losing money, time, energy, or a chance with no lasting benefit. It often describes something that was wasted because the result did not work. The picture is water flowing away and disappearing down a drain.
down-the-line: Something that happens down the line happens later, after the current situation has developed. It can suggest waiting or postponement, and it may also mean farther along in a sequence.
down-the-road: Something that happens down the road will happen at a later time or stage. It often feels less urgent than something happening now, and it is especially common in American English.
drab: Dull and lacking colour, interest, or excitement. People use it for rooms, clothes, moods, styles, or creative work. It sounds blunt, so it may feel rude when describing someone’s personality.
drag-on: Something that drags on continues for longer than people expected or wanted. It often shows mild annoyance with a meeting or delay, though it can be neutral when you are only reporting that it took a long time.
drag-ones-feet: To move forward very slowly when you could act sooner. It often suggests that someone is deliberately delaying, like walking while dragging their feet along the ground.
draw-in: Bring people, customers, or resources into a group or activity. It can mean attracting new members, gaining support, or helping someone become more involved. The image is pulling something toward you or into a group.
draw-the-line: To draw the line is to say clearly that you will not go beyond a certain point. It marks a firm limit and can end a discussion about what is acceptable, though it may sound defensive.
dream-on: Keep hoping for something, even if it is unlikely. It may give support to someone with a big wish, but it can also gently mean they should face facts. The tone changes the message.
dreary: Gloomy, dull, and without energy or cheer. It can describe a sad mood, a tiring day, or long grey surroundings. It often creates a quiet, heavy atmosphere rather than simply saying something is boring.
dregs: Dregs are the least useful bits left after something has been used or removed. The word can mean ordinary leftovers, such as coffee grounds, but it can also insult people by calling them worthless. It is stronger and often older than residue.
dress-down: To dress someone down is to give them a harsh telling-off, often in front of others. It suggests anger or embarrassment more than a calm complaint, and a manager or boss may do it. Do not confuse it with dressing casually, which means wearing informal clothes.
drift-off: Drift off means falling asleep slowly without trying to stay awake. People use it when they are resting, listening, or reading and gradually become sleepy. The image is floating gently away until sleep takes over.
drill-down: When you drill down, you move from a broad subject to smaller parts and exact details. People use it when looking for causes, numbers, or proof. It is like digging through layers instead of staying with the general picture.
drive-a-hard-bargain: Negotiating firmly and pushing for the best possible terms. People use it for tough talks about price, pay, or working conditions. It is stronger than making a fair agreement because it suggests pressure and few easy concessions.
drive-someone-crazy: Drive someone crazy means making them so annoyed or worried that they lose patience. It is an informal, intense expression and usually does not mean a real health problem. The image is causing someone to behave as if they have lost their mind.
drop-in: To drop in means to visit someone briefly, usually without making a plan first. The picture is someone quickly coming into a place for a short time. It sounds friendly and casual, and it can also describe an unexpected visit.
drop-off: To drop off someone or something means to leave them at a place during a quick stop. It can also mean to decrease slowly, such as activity becoming less strong over time. This is different from drop in, which means to visit casually.
drop-the-ball: If you drop the ball, you fail to do something you were responsible for, often because you forgot or missed it. It can also mean making a careless mistake. The image of a falling ball suggests failing to catch or pick something up.
drudgery: Drudgery is dull work that must be repeated again and again. It may need effort, but it gives little interest or pleasure. People often use it for boring jobs, chores, or long tasks.
drum-into: To tell someone something again and again until they understand and remember it. The picture is someone playing the same rhythm on a drum over and over. People use it for important rules, lessons, or safety advice, often with a slightly impatient tone.
dry-out: To dry out is to lose water and become dry, or to become quieter and less energetic. The literal picture is a cloth or piece of land losing all its moisture. People also use it when a person seems to lose their usual energy or enthusiasm.
dry-run: A dry run is a practice before the real activity happens. It helps people find problems and get ready. It may be a simple rehearsal or a full test under normal conditions, but nothing final takes place.
dubious: Dubious means uncertain or doubtful about something. People use it when a fact, result, or plan seems strange or unreliable. It can show mild distrust without directly accusing or confronting someone.
due-course: Something happens in due course at the right time, after any needed steps are finished. It is a polite and reassuring way to say that something will happen naturally later. It does not give an exact date.
dulcet: A dulcet sound is soft, sweet, and pleasing, especially a voice or musical tone. It is often paired with voice, sound, or tones and sounds old-fashioned in everyday speech.
duly-noted: This is a careful and official way to say that a point has been understood. It is often used in reports or replies, and sometimes carries a little sarcasm when the speaker has little interest in the point. It is more formal than simply saying noted.
duplicity: Duplicity is dishonest behaviour in which someone pretends to be genuine while hiding their real aims. It often suggests careful deception over time. This word sounds serious and formal, so it suits professional or serious situations better than everyday arguments.
duress: Duress is pressure that forces someone to act against their wishes. It is stronger than ordinary pressure and can include threats or force. Lawyers often use it when talking about contracts or signatures made without free agreement.
dust-settles: A tense or exciting situation begins to calm down. After that, people can better see the facts and understand what happened. It does not always mean the problem is fully solved.
duty-calls: When duty calls, you must attend to a responsibility or duty. It can sound serious, but people also use it humorously for an unwanted job. It often means personal plans must wait for the task.
dyed-in-the-wool: A belief or habit that is dyed in the wool has become a deep and lasting part of someone. It is stronger than a passing preference and often shapes how that person thinks and acts. The color has gone so deeply into the wool that it cannot easily be removed.
each-to-their-own: People are free to choose or act in the way that suits them best. It shows respect for different needs and preferences. Unlike every man for himself, it does not suggest that people should ignore others.
eagle-eye: An eagle eye notices small details, changes, and mistakes that others may miss. The picture uses the sharp eyesight of an eagle to suggest careful, quick observation. It is usually a compliment, though it can also suggest that someone is watching very closely.
early-bird: Someone who gets up early or acts before everyone else. It is often a friendly way to praise someone for being ready and having an advantage.
earn-ones-keep: To earn one’s keep is to be useful enough to pay for the support you receive. People say it about workers, pets, or tools that give good value. It can sound practical or slightly critical, like saying someone must justify their cost.
ears-are-burning: You feel embarrassed because you think people are talking about you or noticing something private. The hot feeling in your ears brings the idea of shame or embarrassment. It is often used in a playful way.
earth-to-someone: This is a playful call to get someone's attention when they seem far away in thought. It often comes with joking words, but the real meaning is simply pay attention. In serious talks, it may sound too light.
easier-said-than-done: Talking about a solution can be much easier than putting it into practice. People use this when a plan sounds simple but is actually hard to carry out.
easy-come-easy-go: Something that arrives easily can also disappear or be spent quickly. People often use it about money, prizes or chances that do not last. The literal idea is simple: what comes easily also goes easily.
easy-does-it: This tells someone to handle a difficult situation slowly, gently and carefully. It is often used when things are tense or likely to go wrong. It is more direct than take it easy because it gives advice on how to act.
easy-mark: A person who is easy to trick, so others take advantage of them. The tone is often a little mocking, so use it carefully about someone you know. The picture is a soft target that a swindler can pick out of the crowd.
easy-money: Easy money is income that comes with little effort, time, or risk. The phrase can describe a quick, simple job, but it often hints that the money may not last or may come from a questionable deal. It is often confused with a guaranteed, long-term income.
eat-crow: To eat crow is to admit that you were wrong after your actions or claims failed. It can feel humiliating, blunt, or teasing, especially when someone has argued confidently and lost. The unpleasant image of eating a crow comes from an old idea of defeat and shame.
eat-the-rich: This slogan says that rich people should give up some of their wealth so others can benefit. The image of eating them is deliberately shocking and violent. It is blunt political criticism and may sound hostile.
ebullient: Full of lively energy, excitement, and enthusiasm. A person can be ebullient, and a party or atmosphere can feel the same way. It suggests happiness that is hard to hold back.
eclectic: Eclectic describes a choice of many different styles, sources, or traditions. It often suggests curiosity and an open mind rather than loyalty to one narrow approach. An eclectic collection might mix old and new designs.
edifice: An edifice is a large, impressive building, but it can also mean a planned system of ideas or institutions. This second use is formal and often suggests something grand but hard to change. In normal speech, building or structure is easier.
efficacy: Efficacy tells us how well something works and produces the wanted result. It is often used for medicine, research, and methods. It is a more formal word for effectiveness.
effigy: An effigy is a model or image of a person. People may make one to criticise or punish someone symbolically, often by burning it. The phrase burn in effigy is common in political news.
effrontery: Effrontery is shameless behaviour that ignores respect, rules, or what is acceptable. People use this strong word when someone is bold in a clearly improper way. It is much stronger than cheeky and carries strong disapproval.
egg-on: To egg someone on is to urge or push them to do something. Among friends it may be playful, but it can also mean pressure or deliberate provocation. It is close to encourage, but often suggests that the other person needs a push.
egotist: An egotist is too focused on their own worth, success, or importance. This behaviour can make them self-centred and hard to work with. Unlike ordinary confidence, an egotist usually sees other people as less important.
egregious: An egregious act is extremely bad, shocking, or careless in a way that demands attention. It is stronger than bad and often suggests that the situation is unusually serious.
elaborate: Elaborate means carefully made with many details or steps. It can be positive when it shows careful planning, but negative when it seems too complicated. As a verb, it also means to give more details about something.
elapse: This describes a period of time passing and coming to an end. People often use it for deadlines, journeys, or events. It is a formal alternative to pass in expressions such as time elapsed.
elephant-in-the-room: An elephant in the room is a serious problem that everyone knows about but nobody wants to discuss. It can describe the problem itself or the group's habit of ignoring it. The huge animal makes the image clear: pretending it is not there does not make it disappear.
eleventh-hour: At the last possible moment, just before a deadline or event. It often suggests that the action was delayed longer than it should have been.
elicit: To elicit something is to draw it out, often by asking a careful question. People use it for answers, facts, or reactions in research and work. It is different from reveal, because the goal is to get a response.
eloquent: An eloquent person says ideas clearly and in a moving or convincing way. We praise speeches, arguments, and writing as eloquent when they sound powerful and easy to follow. It is more than simply correct grammar.
elucidate: To elucidate something is to explain it clearly so others can understand it. You often see it in academic or professional writing, where it is a formal way of saying explain or clarify. It suggests that the subject was hard to understand before.
elusive: Elusive describes something that is hard to find, catch, reach, or understand. The difficulty often lasts, rather than happening just once. People may also call a person elusive when they are difficult to pin down.
emaciated: Extremely thin because of hunger, illness, or poor nutrition describes an emaciated person or animal. It is a serious and sometimes upsetting word, often used in medical reports or historical accounts.
emanating: Something emanating comes from a source and spreads outward. We use it for light, smells, sounds, feelings, or influence coming from a person or place. It is more literary than simply coming from.
embellish: Embellishing means adding attractive or impressive details to a story, design, or idea. The details may be true, but they can also make something seem better or richer than it is. People often confuse it with exaggerating, which means making something seem too large.
eminent: An eminent person is well known and respected because of excellent work or abilities. It often describes standing in a field, while famous may only mean widely known.
emissary: An emissary is someone sent to speak for another person or group. The role is official and authorised, and it often appears in political, business, or old stories. Envoy is similar, but emissary can sound more formal and dramatic.
emit: To send out light, heat, sound, gas, radiation, or a smell is to emit it. This is more technical than give off, but it can also mean expressing an opinion or emotion in a formal way.
empathetic: Able to understand and share another person’s feelings. Someone empathetic listens and tries to see the situation from the other person’s view. It does not always mean they agree with that person.
emulate: To emulate someone is to copy their behaviour, style, or method because you admire them. It often means trying to match their success or qualities, not just their clothes. A common word connected to it is role model.
encomium: A formal speech or piece of writing that praises someone or something very warmly. It sounds grand and literary, and it may praise the person more strongly than seems necessary.
encroach: To encroach is to move slowly into someone’s time, space, rights, or land without permission. It often suggests an unwanted advance that becomes harder to stop. This is different from intrude, which can happen suddenly.
encumbrance: An encumbrance is a burden that makes an action or property harder to use or sell. In law, it may be a claim on property. In everyday speech, it simply means an annoying complication, like encumbrance on travel.
end-of-story: The matter is settled, so there is no need to discuss it again. People use this when they want to end a debate. It sounds firm and slightly impatient, so use it carefully.
end-of-the-world: The end of the world means a situation feels so terrible or overwhelming that nothing seems possible. People use it to show strong distress, often with exaggeration. It is different from saying the world will really end.
energetic: An energetic person has lots of energy, enthusiasm, and lively movement. We also use it for activities that are full of excitement and effort. It is usually positive, though it can sometimes suggest someone is restless or overly intense.
enervated: Weakened and drained of energy, often because of illness or hard work. It sounds more formal than exhausted. It can also mean that something has been made less strong or effective.
engrossed: So focused on something that your full attention is on it. It shows a stronger and longer interest than simply being interested. It can also mean that a task or situation takes up all your attention.
enhance: To enhance something is to make it better in quality, value, or appearance. People use it when talking about improving features, performance, or a reputation. It sounds positive and suggests a real improvement.
enigma: An enigma is a person, event, or thing that is hard to understand. It suggests a puzzle that may eventually be solved and often adds mystery or drama. Unlike a simple mistake, an enigma has a deeper and more lasting feeling of secrecy.
ennui: A deep feeling of boredom and dissatisfaction with life. It is more serious and thoughtful than ordinary boredom, as if nothing seems worth caring about. It is often used when discussing art, literature, or unhappy lives.
enough-is-enough: Something has gone far enough and should stop now. People use it to set a clear limit about noise, work, or behaviour. It can sound impatient or annoyed, so the tone matters.
enough-said: What was just said is clear, so more talk is not needed. It can show that you understand and accept the point. It may sound abrupt, especially in a serious conversation.
entourage: An entourage is the group of people who regularly go with and support someone important or famous. It often includes assistants, advisers, and friends. The word can sound admiring, but it is more formal than the usual group of people.
entreaty: An entreaty is a serious, emotional request for help or agreement. It sounds more emotional and respectful than a normal request, often because the person is in a difficult situation. It is not the same as a command or a complaint.
enunciate: To say words clearly, giving each syllable its full sound. People use it for careful speech or for stating an idea clearly. It sounds more formal than pronounce, which is the everyday word.
ephemeral: Something that lasts only a short time is ephemeral. It can sound a little poetic and sad, but in technology it simply means temporary, like a message that disappears. Unlike brief, it often gives a feeling of beauty or loss.
epithet: A word or short phrase that describes someone in a memorable way, such as a label or nickname. It can be admiring or insulting, but it often has a sharp, negative meaning in modern English.
epitome: An epitome is the clearest example of a wider group, type, or idea. People often use it with approval to show how well one thing represents many others. It can also mean a short summary of a larger subject.
equanimity: Staying calm and steady during a difficult or tense situation. It means you can think clearly without becoming angry, upset, or flustered. It is often used to praise mature and professional behaviour.
eradicate: Removing a disease, pest, or harmful practice for good is the main idea here. It is stronger than reduce or end because it suggests getting rid of the source. Pollution and corruption are often described this way.
err-on-the-side-of-caution: When results are uncertain, choose the safer choice even if it seems very careful. The image is one side of a path: caution is the safer side to take instead of the risky one.
erudite: Erudite describes someone with broad learning and a curious, active mind. It is a polite, complimentary word, but it sounds more formal than learned. It suggests deeper knowledge rather than simply knowing many facts.
eruption: A sudden burst of lava, sound, emotion, or activity is an eruption. It can describe a physical release, such as a skin rash, or an outburst of anger or laughter. The usual picture is something suddenly bursting out.
escalation: An escalation is a problem that grows more serious, intense, or difficult to control. It may describe a conflict, a response, or an issue passed to higher management. Unlike an increase, it often suggests that things are getting worse.
eschew: When you choose on purpose to keep away from something, you eschew it. People use it for things they could easily do but decide to avoid, like eschewing rich food or fancy words. It sounds a bit formal. Do not confuse it with ignore, which just means not paying attention.
ethics: Ethics are the principles people use to judge what is right, wrong, or fair. These can be personal beliefs or rules followed in a job, such as medicine or business. Morals is similar, but ethics often focuses on fair choices and professional duties.
euphemism: A soft or indirect word used instead of something blunt, private, or unpleasant. People use it to make bad news sound gentler, but it can also seem like hiding the truth. It is often confused with a polite phrase.
evaluate: To evaluate is to judge something after thinking it over, using facts or evidence. You might evaluate a new phone, a student's work, or how well a plan worked. It is more careful than just liking or disliking something. Evaluate and assess mean almost the same thing.
evanescent: Beauty, joy, or interest can be evanescent when it lasts only a very short time and then fades. It sounds more literary than everyday words like brief, and it is often used for lovely but short-lived things.
even-keel: An even keel means a steady, balanced state with things under control. The literal image is a ship floating level instead of leaning to one side. People often say a project is back on an even keel after problems improve.
even-money: Even money describes a situation where both outcomes are equally likely. It comes from betting with the same amount on each side, and people often say it when they feel very sure something will happen.
eventuate: Something eventuates when it happens as the result of earlier actions or changes. The word sounds formal and focuses on the connection between causes and results. People also use it for events that were expected but not fully planned.
everything-and-the-kitchen-sink: People use this to say that something includes every extra thing, even useless ones. It often has a slightly funny or critical tone. The picture is a kitchen sink holding every tool and object you could imagine.
everything-but-the-kitchen-sink: People use this when they mean a huge number of things, tools, problems, or choices, often more than they can manage. It can sound joking or complainative. The image is every kitchen object except the sink, which is famously used for washing.
everything-under-the-sun: All the different things that exist or could be imagined. People use it when they want to say there is a huge range of possibilities. The sun shines over the whole world, so its literal picture suggests everything in the world.
evince: Evince means to show clearly that something exists or is true. It is often used for results, actions, or qualities that give proof. This formal word is stronger than simply showing something, and it should not be confused with evoke, which means to bring out a feeling.
exacerbate: A problem gets worse when something makes it harder to deal with. Exacerbate is a formal word for adding to an already bad situation, such as stress that makes pain more severe.
exacting: An exacting person or task demands careful work and precise results. It can be a compliment about high standards, but it may also mean someone is hard to please. It is stronger than strict because it focuses closely on details and quality.
excoriate: To criticize someone or something in a very harsh and detailed way. It is stronger than criticize and suggests that the speaker leaves no weakness unmentioned.
excruciating: Pain this intense is almost unbearable. People use it for terrible physical pain, deep emotional suffering, or a very difficult experience. It is stronger and more dramatic than simply saying something hurts.
excuse-me: This polite phrase gets someone’s attention, asks for space, or shows a small apology. You might use it before a question or after a small mistake. How it feels depends on your tone and the situation.
exhort: To urge someone strongly to do something or stop doing it. People use it for serious advice or a warning, often in a stern voice. Urge is a more common and less formal word.
exonerate: To exonerate someone means to officially clear them of blame or declare that they did not deserve punishment. Evidence or an official decision may do this. It is broader than an acquittal, which is a formal decision that someone is not guilty.
expatriate: An expatriate is someone living outside their home country, often because of work. It can also suggest that the person has moved to a place with a different culture. In everyday speech, expat is shorter and more common.
expedite: To expedite a task is to make it happen faster. It is common in work messages when someone asks for a delivery, approval, or request to be moved forward. It shows urgency without sounding rude.
expunge: Expunge means to remove a record or statement completely, often through an official process. People use it for files, histories, and databases, and the word sounds more final than erase. It is usually stronger and more formal than delete.
expurgate: To remove private, unsuitable, or upsetting parts from a text. It is often used for careful edits before a book, film, or other work is released. It is more formal than clean or edit.
extant: Something extant still exists, often because it has survived from an earlier time. People use it for old texts, artworks, animals, or records. It is more common in careful or historical writing than in everyday speech.
extenuating: Extenuating describes reasons that make an action or mistake seem less serious or blameworthy. The common phrase is extenuating circumstances, which explains why someone acted in a particular way. It reduces blame, but it does not completely remove responsibility.
extinct: No longer existing as a species is the main meaning of extinct. It can also describe something no longer active, such as an old volcano, disease, tradition, or product line. The word often feels final and permanent.
extol: To praise someone or something with great admiration, often in a speech, review, or formal text. It sounds stronger and more careful than the ordinary word praise.
extortion: Extortion is getting money, property, or a benefit by threats or improper pressure. It is a serious abuse of power and is common in legal and news reporting. It is different from theft because the victim gives something under pressure.
extraneous: Extraneous describes things that are not needed and do not belong to the main subject. If a report has extra charts that help nothing, those charts are extraneous. People also say extraneous information, like details that add clutter. It is the opposite of relevant and germane.
extravagant: An extravagant choice uses much more money, effort, or detail than it really needs. It often sounds critical, especially when describing showy spending, parties, clothes, or behaviour.
extrinsic: Something extrinsic comes from outside the activity itself, such as money, praise, or pressure. People use it to describe outside reasons for doing something. It is the opposite of intrinsic, which comes from enjoyment or interest in the activity itself.
exult: To celebrate with very strong feelings and excitement is to exult. It is often used after a major victory or happy achievement. It is more dramatic and energetic than simply celebrating.
exultation: Exultation is a sudden burst of great joy or triumph. It often appears in stories about winning, achieving something important, or receiving excellent news. It is stronger and more dramatic than happiness.
eye-for-an-eye: An eye for an eye means that someone should receive punishment that matches the harm they caused. It can sound fair and firm, but it may also suggest revenge. The literal idea of losing an eye for losing an eye shows punishment in equal measure.
fabricate: Fabricating can mean making or building something, but it often means inventing a false story, document, or claim. Context shows which meaning is intended. When it refers to dishonesty, it is similar to forge, especially in formal writing about evidence or documents.
face-facts: Facing facts means accepting a hard truth instead of hiding from it. People use it after a loss, mistake, or problem that cannot be changed. Imagine looking straight at the facts instead of turning away, so the phrase can feel direct and uncomfortable.
face-the-music: To face the music is to accept the bad results of something you did or decided. You use it when a mistake, cost, or embarrassment can no longer be avoided. The image comes from stepping onto a stage to perform while the music plays.
face-value: Face value is the amount printed on a bond, note, or other financial paper. In everyday use, at face value means accepting what someone says without checking it. It is not the same as the current market price, which can be higher or lower.
facet: A facet is one side or part of a bigger thing. We talk about facets of a personality, facets of a problem, or facets of a diamond. In geometry and gems, it means a flat surface. It is a formal word for feature or aspect, and it often goes with of.
facetious: Humorous and playful, often in a way that gently makes fun of something. It works best in relaxed conversations or creative work. On a serious subject, it can sound careless or hurtful.
facile: Facile means easy to do or easy to understand, usually without much effort. A facile solution sounds neat and quick. Be careful: when critics use it, they often mean too easy, with no real depth. It is similar to facile in French, meaning quick or skillful.
factitious: Factitious means invented or carefully arranged rather than based on real life or facts. People may call a story, claim, or system factitious when it lacks naturalness or truth. It is easy to confuse with fictitious, which also means invented but does not stress careful arrangement.
factor-in: To factor in something means to include it when making a decision or judgment. You are treating it as important, rather than leaving it out. People often use it with factors such as cost, time, risk, or needs.
fade-out: Images, sounds, and even people can fade out by becoming slowly weaker or less important until they are hard to notice. Use it when something disappears gradually rather than stopping suddenly. The word fade shows this slow loss of strength or visibility.
fair-enough: Fair enough shows that you accept another person’s point as reasonable. It often ends a small disagreement, though it can sound a little impatient if the issue is still serious. The literal idea is that the response or standard is fair, so you agree it makes sense.
fair-is-fair: Everyone should be treated by the same rule. You say this when you believe a decision was fair and nobody received special treatment. It can sound confident, but also argumentative if someone sees things differently.
fair-play: Fair play means doing things honestly and giving everyone a fair chance. In sports, players must follow the rules rather than cheat. The same idea can describe work decisions and relationships, though it may sound accusing during a disagreement.
fair-share: A fair share is the equal or reasonable part of work, resources, blame, or responsibility that someone should get. People use it to say they have done their proper share. It sometimes carries a hint that other people have done less.
fairs-fair: Both sides should accept the outcome because the same rule applies to each one. It has a practical British feel and suggests there should be no special treatment. It can sound impatient if you push it too hard.
fall-apart: Something falls apart when it breaks into pieces, stops working, or becomes too difficult to manage emotionally. It often suggests a steady collapse, not one sudden accident. People also say this when a person starts crying or losing control.
fall-behind: To become slower or less advanced than another person or group. You may have missed a lesson, done less work, or not moved forward as quickly.
fall-for: Falling for something means being tricked by it, especially a scam or a trick. Falling for someone means becoming attracted to them, often in a romantic way. The object of the verb helps show which meaning is meant.
fall-short: To fall short means to miss an expected result, level, or standard. You might say the sales fell short of the goal because they were lower than expected. It points to a clear gap, not simply trying and failing.
fallacious: A fallacious idea is built on faulty thinking, so the conclusion may look right but the reasoning is wrong. A fallacious argument is a common subject in debate and law. It is stronger than just doubtful, and it is not the same as a fallacy, which is the faulty argument itself.
false-alarm: A false alarm is a warning about danger when there is no real danger. The image is an alarm ringing for no reason, and it can also mean a worry or complaint that later proves wrong.
falter: To falter is to stop going smoothly, usually because of doubt, tiredness, or a hard moment. A speaker may falter halfway through a speech, and a team may falter in the last minutes. It can also describe walking unsteadily. Compare it with hesitate, which is similar.
far-and-away: Far and away means much more than the other choices. If one team wins far and away, it wins by a clearly large amount. The phrase often follows a superlative, such as the best or the most popular.
far-be-it: Far be it says strongly that something is not true or intended. It often follows from me or from us, then a word like to complain. The picture of keeping something far away makes the denial emphatic and sometimes formal.
far-cry: A far cry describes a big difference between what you have now and what you expected or remember. It often shows that the change is far from what you hoped for. The picture of a cry coming from far away makes the distance between two things clear.
farm-out: To farm out a task means to give it to someone else, often an outside worker. The person or company receiving it takes on the work and much of the responsibility. It is common in business, but it can sound dismissive about a team member.
fastidious: A fastidious person is extremely careful about details, accuracy, and proper order. The word can praise thorough work, but it may also suggest someone is hard to please. It is stronger than careful and often describes someone who notices every small mistake.
fatal: Fatal means causing death, or serious enough to destroy a plan or result. It is stronger than bad or serious and suggests that the damage cannot be repaired. People often use it with words like error, flaw, and injury.
fatuous: Showing foolish thought and often silly self-importance. It is a sharp, formal criticism, so it can sound stronger and more personal than simply saying someone was foolish.
feasible: A plan is feasible when there is enough time, money, and help to make it happen. People use it when checking what can really be done, not just what sounds good in theory. Not feasible is often a polite way to say no.
fed-up: Fed up means having no more patience or interest in something that has continued too long. People use it about repeated problems, difficult people, or tiring tasks. The literal image is eating until you feel full and cannot eat any more.
feel-free: Feel free gives someone permission to act, ask questions, or make their own choices. It sounds friendly and encouraging, often when offering help. It is polite but not as firm or official as a direct instruction.
feel-out: Feeling someone out means testing what they think or want without asking too directly. People use it when checking interest, support, or reaction to an idea. It is a cautious move, and it is gentler than asking someone straight out.
feint: A feint is a false move, statement, or appearance made to draw attention away from the real plan. People use it in sports, strategy, and stories when the goal is to fool or surprise someone. It is clever in a game but can also sound dishonest.
felicitous: Describing a happy accident or a choice that fits a situation especially well. It sounds polished and literary, and it often praises a result or expression that came at just the right moment.
felon: A felon is someone who has been found guilty of a serious crime. This is mainly a legal word and can sound harsh, while criminal is a more neutral way to describe a person who broke the law.
fervid: Fervid shows very strong excitement, passion, or support for something. It can sound admiring, as in strong enthusiasm, but it may also suggest that the feelings are too intense or heated. It is often used in formal writing.
fetish: A fetish is an unusually strong interest in or attraction to something. In general English, it can mean a strong passion for an object or activity. In psychology and adult contexts, it can mean a strong sexual attraction to a particular thing or type of person.
fiasco: A complete failure, especially one that is public, embarrassing, or far worse than expected. It is more dramatic than saying something failed, so use it for a major disaster.
fiat: A fiat is a firm order from someone with official power. People use it for orders by governments, courts or business leaders, and it suggests that the order must be obeyed.
fight-fire-with-fire: You meet a hard or hostile problem with an equally strong response. People use it for arguments, negotiations, or competition, but it may also warn that both sides are making the situation worse.
fill-in: To fill in can mean adding missing information to a form or short blank space. It can also mean taking another person’s place for a short time. The exact meaning depends on what you are filling or who you are replacing.
final-say: One person or group has the last power to approve, reject, or decide something. It is used after others have shared their views and the matter is ready for a final choice.
fine-line: A fine line is a very small difference between two similar things. People use it when the gap is easy to miss but the results are quite different. Imagine a thin drawn line: crossing it may look harmless, but it can lead somewhere quite wrong.
fine-print: Fine print means the small words in a contract or agreement that may hide important limits or conditions. People usually mention it when something costly appears only in those small details. It often goes with read, check, or ignore.
fingers-crossed: Crossing your fingers shows hope that an uncertain result will go well. People use it with friends, family, or colleagues when they cannot control what will happen, so the feeling is hopeful but careful.
first-come-first-served: People are served or treated in the order they arrive. There are no exceptions, even for people who want special treatment. People use it for tickets, shops, queues or any fair order based on arrival.
first-things-first: The most important or urgent matter should be handled before anything else. It sounds practical and can gently tell someone to change their order of work. The literal idea is that the first matters come before later ones.
flabbergasted: Being flabbergasted means being so surprised that you cannot believe what you have heard. The reaction is sudden and often linked to shocking or strange news. It sounds more dramatic than simply being surprised.
flagrant: So clear, shocking, or wrong that nobody can easily ignore it. It often describes deliberate bad behavior, an obvious mistake, or unfairness, and it carries a strong negative feeling.
flamboyant: A flamboyant person or style is bright, dramatic, and impossible to ignore. It can mean confident self-expression, but it can also suggest showing off and wanting attention. It is stronger than colourful and often describes clothes, behaviour, or design.
flashy: Designed to catch attention with bright colors, bold details, or a big display. It can suggest something exciting and impressive, but also something too showy or not very practical.
flay: To attack someone or something with fierce criticism and expose every weakness. It is stronger than criticize, and the violent picture of removing skin makes the verb feel very harsh.
fledgling: A fledgling is a new worker or beginner who has promise but still needs to learn. People also use it for a young bird that has not learned to fly, so it suggests being young and not yet able to do everything.
fleeting: Something fleeting lasts only a short time and quickly passes. It often describes emotions, thoughts, chances, or moments. Unlike brief, it has a slightly poetic feel and stresses that the thing will soon disappear.
