keep-it-together: Staying calm and in control during a hard or stressful moment is called keeping it together. People often say it to encourage someone to focus and manage their feelings. The image is of keeping loose pieces together in one place.
keep-me-in-the-loop: Tell me what is happening, even if I am not directly involved. People use this at work when they want updates and feel included. It is the opposite of being out of the loop, which means being left out.
keep-ones-fingers-crossed: Keep your fingers crossed is a light way to hope for a good result while you wait. The crossed-finger sign is an old picture of good luck, and it shows hope mixed with uncertainty, not a sure promise.
keep-ones-head-above-water: To keep one’s head above water is to keep managing when money, energy, or stability is limited. It describes surviving a difficult time, not being completely comfortable. The image comes from swimming and staying above the surface.
keep-someone-in-the-loop: To keep someone in the loop means to tell them what is happening as plans or work develop. It is not enough to give them the final result, because they may need updates. It comes from keeping someone inside the informed circle.
kettle-of-fish: A kettle of fish is a messy situation with several problems tied together. The image is a crowded kettle full of fish. It is often used when something that seemed simple has become confusing or difficult to manage.
kick-off: To kick off is to begin a meeting, event, discussion, or activity. The image comes from kicking the ball to start a football match. It sounds informal and energetic, so it suits clear activities and events.
kick-the-bucket: Dying is described in a joking or informal way with this phrase. The image is someone kicking a bucket as their life ends. It may sound funny, but it can hurt people, so use it carefully in serious situations.
kicking-and-screaming: People use this when they complain loudly and strongly against a change or decision. The image of someone kicking and screaming shows obvious, often playful resistance. It is similar to saying someone is making a big fuss.
kill-two-birds-with-one-stone: One action can give you two good results when you use this phrase. The literal picture is one stone killing two birds, so it shows how you can handle two tasks together. People use it when a choice or plan saves time and effort.
knee-jerk-reaction: You react immediately from instinct instead of stopping to think. People use it for quick decisions or comments that ignore the wider situation, usually with mild criticism.
knell: A knell is the deep, serious sound of a ringing bell, often for mourning or death. The word can also mean a warning that something is ending. It has a heavy, traditional feeling and sounds more dramatic than just bell.
knock-it-out-of-the-park: You do a task better than expected, and everyone is excited about the result. It comes from baseball: hitting the ball so hard that it flies out of the park.
know-every-trick-in-the-book: You know all the methods, shortcuts, and skills in a job or subject when you use this phrase. The picture comes from knowing every trick in an instruction book. It may praise your experience, but it can also suggest that you know how to use the rules in clever ways.
know-inside-and-out: To know something inside and out means you understand every part of it and how it works. People say it about a system, skill, or person when their knowledge is very deep. It is stronger than simply knowing something.
labyrinth: A labyrinth is a complicated set of passages with many turns, or a situation that is hard to understand and solve. The word suggests you need patience and careful choices to find your way. It sounds more formal than maze, which often refers to a physical puzzle or design.
laceration: A laceration is a deep cut or tear in the skin, often caused by a sharp or rough object. Medical and workplace reports use it for more serious injuries than a simple cut. The wound may have uneven edges and damage nearby tissue.
lackluster: Lackluster describes a performance, event, or result that is dull and does not create excitement. It may still have some good points, so it is less final than saying something is a failure. It often sounds calm and measured.
laconic: A laconic reply or style uses very few words to communicate clearly. The shortness feels deliberate, not lazy or rude, although it may seem cool to some people. It is similar to concise, but it puts more emphasis on using only a few words.
large-as-life: Someone or something can appear so clear and noticeable that people say it is as big as life. It can also mean that a person is truly there in person. The tone is often amused or strongly emphatic.
largess: Largess means generous giving of money, gifts, or valuable things. It often suggests the gift is especially noticeable, or that the giver expects thanks. The word sounds a little formal and can sometimes imply a show of generosity.
lassitude: This is a heavy, empty feeling with no energy or interest in doing anything. It can come from being very tired, or from a dull afternoon that drags on. The everyday word is tiredness, and this one sounds formal and bookish.
last-hired-first-fired: When a workplace cuts jobs, this phrase names the idea that the newest worker may leave first. Imagine workers standing in a line by hiring date, with the newest at the end. It is not a rule everywhere; company policy and local law also matter.
last-i-checked: Your information may be out of date, and this phrase shows that you know only what was true when you last checked. It is casual and careful. People often use it to correct an assumption without sounding too sure.
last-mile: This is the final part of getting something to its destination or making it work in practice. It often points to the difficult last steps, such as local delivery or turning a plan into action.
last-minute: A last-minute action happens at the very end, with little time left to prepare. It can suggest urgency or poor planning, but it may only describe the timing. Use last-minute with a hyphen before a noun, such as last-minute plans.
last-time-i-checked: You are giving the most recent information you have, but you do not promise that it is still true. People use it when the facts may have changed, often to gently correct an assumption.
late-in-the-game: Near the end of a game, when there is very little time left to act. People use it when a problem could have been fixed earlier, but now the chance to fix it well is almost gone.
latent: A latent problem, risk, or ability is already there but hidden or not yet developed. It may become clear or active later under the right conditions. People often use it to describe threats that have not fully appeared.
laudable: Laudable describes an action, effort, or decision that deserves praise because it is good or helpful. It sounds respectful and is often used in formal reports or reviews. It is a more serious way of saying that something is commendable.
lavish: Generous, rich, or plentiful in an impressive way. It can praise generous praise or hospitality, but it can also suggest waste and excess, so context decides whether it sounds warm or negative.
lax: Lax means not strict or careful enough about rules, duties, or details. It can describe a relaxed person or weak controls, and it is often confused with lenient, which focuses more on allowing mistakes.
legerdemain: Legerdemain is skillful deception or trickery used to fool people. The old picture comes from magicians making things seem to disappear and reappear by hand. Today it usually refers to cunning tricks in business or politics.
leisurely: A leisurely action is done slowly, calmly, and without hurry. It describes a relaxed pace for travel, work, or conversation. It can also hint that something is taking too long, so context matters.
lend-a-hand: Giving someone a helping hand is the main idea here. The literal image is extending your hand so another person can take it. People use it for small, quick acts of help, often in a friendly way.
lenient: Lenient means not strict about rules, mistakes, or required standards. It can show a fair and understanding attitude, but it may also suggest that important standards are being allowed to slip.
lesser-of-two-evils: The lesser of two evils is the less harmful choice when both options are bad. It is often used to explain a difficult decision that nobody is happy about. People use it when they need to compare drawbacks and pick the smaller problem.
let-that-sink-in: Let that sink in means to pause and think carefully about what you have just heard or seen. People use it when a fact or comment needs time to be fully understood, like water slowly soaking into the ground.
let-the-cat-out-of-the-bag: A secret comes out, usually by accident, and can no longer be hidden. The funny image is of a cat jumping from an open bag, so the secret slips out carelessly.
let-the-grass-grow-under-ones-feet: Standing still for so long that grass grows around your feet shows how long you have wasted time. People use it when they delay a task or avoid a responsibility. It often suggests that the delay could easily have been avoided.
let-them-eat-cake: A rich person is imagined as saying that hungry people should be happy with cake. The phrase shows a careless attitude toward what poor people really need, and is often used when talking about unfairness.
lethal: A lethal thing can easily cause death. People use this word for strong drugs, dangerous weapons, or harmful animals. It describes the power to kill, while fatal is more often used when someone has actually died.
lethargic: This describes someone with very little energy or interest, moving slowly and wanting to do nothing. It can last for hours or even days, unlike a quick tired feeling. It is close to listless, and people often say sluggish too.
lets-face-it: You are bringing out a truth that people may be trying to avoid. It helps the talk become honest and move toward solving a problem, though repeating it can sound impatient.
levity: This is light, playful humour, often used when a situation is serious or tense. A joke during a hard meeting can bring levity and help people relax. It is different from jocose, because levity is more about the moment, and it sounds a little formal.
lie-low: You lie low when you stay quiet and avoid getting attention. The picture is of staying close to the ground and out of sight. People use it when waiting for danger to pass or when they do not want others to notice them.
light-at-the-end-of-the-tunnel: A hard period is still happening, but you can see that it will end soon. The image is daylight at the far end of a dark tunnel, so it gives a small feeling of hope.
line-in-the-sand: You make a clear limit and warn that you will not accept what goes beyond it. People use it to show where acceptable behaviour ends and serious consequences begin.
lions-share: A lion’s share is the largest or most important part of something that is shared. It can simply describe the result, but it may also suggest that one person took far more than the others. The image is the lion claiming the biggest part of its prey.
liquidation: Liquidation is the formal process of closing a business and paying its debts by selling what it owns. It often sounds final because the business is ending. People may confuse it with a liquidation sale, when goods are sold to clear remaining stock.
lithe: Lithe describes a body that moves easily, smoothly, and with grace. People often use it for dancers, athletes, or animals. It is more about graceful movement than ordinary flexibility.
live-rent-free-in-someones-head: Someone lives rent-free in your head when you cannot stop thinking about them. The phrase can mean that they have made a strong impression, but it often has an annoyed edge when they are irritating. It is similar to being unforgettable, but not always in a good way.
livid: In everyday use this means extremely angry, with strong emotion inside. It can also describe skin that looks dark blue or purple, like a bruise. People often confuse it with vivid, which means bright and clear in colour.
loath: You are loath to do something when you really do not want to do it. It is stronger and more formal than “reluctant,” and it usually appears as “loath to” plus an action; do not confuse it with “loathe,” which means to hate something.
loathe: To loathe something is to hate it very deeply, often with a strong feeling of disgust or fear. People use it for things that feel awful or unbearable, not just things they do not enjoy. It is stronger than dislike, but often a little less extreme than saying you hate something.
lock-horns: Two sides argue, compete, or confront each other directly. It suggests a strong clash of opinions or interests, rather than a calm discussion with little tension.
long-run: Over a long run, a choice or trend may have a different effect from what it seems like now. People use it when they care about what will happen after the first results, not just the short-term result.
longevity: A long life, or the length of time something remains useful or successful. People often use it for people, products, organizations, or traditions, and it sounds more formal than lifespan or durability.
loom-large: When something looms large, it seems very important or threatening, even if it has not happened yet. The image is a big shape in the distance that fills your view and makes you feel worried.
lord-knows: People use this when nobody can know the answer for sure. It can show surprise, worry, or frustration about what will happen. Asking God to reveal the truth explains why it feels impossible to predict.
low-blow: Someone says or does something cruel, unfair, or disloyal. It often describes an attack on a person’s dignity, work, or reputation, so it feels more personal than normal criticism.
low-hanging-fruit: Low-hanging fruit means the easiest tasks to complete or gains to get. People use it when choosing what to do first, since these tasks often bring quick results with little effort. It can also sound dismissive, as if easy work is not worth much.
low-road: Taking the low road means choosing the easier, less demanding, or less respectable option. The image is a path below the normal level, sometimes a moral shortcut. People also use it when describing a decision that avoids difficult work.
lower-the-bar: The rules or expected quality are made easier, so people need less skill or effort to succeed. This is not the same as raising the bar, which means asking people to do better.
lucid: A lucid explanation or description is clear and easy to understand. The word can also describe a moment when someone's thoughts become clear again. It is similar to clear, but often suggests careful thinking as well as simple words.
lucrative: Lucrative describes work, a business, or an opportunity that makes a lot of money. People often use it when something is especially profitable. It is stronger and more attractive than simply saying successful, but it focuses on money rather than general success.
lugubrious: This describes sadness that feels very heavy, dramatic, or almost too much. People often use it for overly emotional performances or writing, so it can sound a little theatrical rather than truly sorrowful.
lurid: Something lurid is shown in a shocking, intense, or exaggerated way. People use it for details about injuries, crime, or corruption that feel too dramatic to leave out, even if the facts may be true.
lush: Lush describes plants that grow thickly and look rich and healthy. It can also describe soft, beautiful places, sounds, or details. Sometimes it has a slight negative meaning, suggesting something is too rich or excessive.
macabre: This refers to things connected with death, decay, or fear in a grim and unsettling way. It often describes stories, pictures, or humour that makes people feel disturbed, rather than simply describing something sad.
machiavellian: A Machiavellian person or plan is cunning, careful, and ready to use others for personal gain. The word often criticizes manipulative political tactics, not ordinary smart planning. It is stronger and more negative than simply strategic.
mad-as-a-hatter: This describes someone who is unusual, wild, or hard to predict. The old image of a hatter making unusual hats explains the playful idea, but it should not be used as a label for mental illness.
magic-bullet: People use this for a quick, easy answer to a big problem. It often carries a critical tone: there is no magic bullet, so the problem still needs real work and time.
magnanimous: Magnanimous means generous and forgiving, especially when you could feel angry or treat someone harshly. It sounds formal and respectful, while generous is the more common word in everyday speech.
maim: To maim someone is to injure them so badly that they may have lasting damage, especially to a limb. It is stronger than hurt or injure. People also use it for serious damage to buildings, machines, or chances.
make-ends-meet: To make ends meet is to earn just enough money for your bills and basic needs. It often suggests a tight budget with no room for extras. The image is joining two separate ends so that they meet.
make-someones-day: A kind act, good news, or a small surprise can make someone’s day much better. People use it when something gives another person real pleasure, especially during a difficult day. The idea is that the day starts to feel brighter.
make-the-best-of: Make the best of a situation means accepting that it is not perfect and doing as well as you can. People use it during bad luck or when there are few choices. It is similar to making the most of what you have.
make-time: Making time means changing your plans so you have enough time to do something or see someone. It often suggests that the person or task matters enough to give up part of your schedule. It often goes with time for someone or time to do something.
make-up-ones-mind: Making up your mind means reaching a decision and stopping your search for other choices. People use it after thinking something over, or to ask someone to decide. It can sound firm, especially when the person has taken too long to choose.
make-yourself-at-home: Make yourself at home means acting as if you are welcome to relax and use what you need. People say it to guests so they feel comfortable in your home. It can also mean settling in and making a shared place feel easy and relaxed.
maladjusted: Maladjusted describes someone who has difficulty managing emotions, behaviour, or social expectations in daily life. It is a formal and blunt word, so it can sound insulting when used directly about a person.
malady: A malady is a serious illness or health problem that prevents normal life. The word sounds old-fashioned and fits formal or literary writing more than everyday speech. People may also use it for a serious social problem.
malevolent: A malevolent person wants to hurt or damage others. It is stronger than words like unkind or unfriendly because it points to clear bad intentions.
malignant: A malignant tumour can spread and cause serious harm. In other situations, malignant means deliberately harmful or hostile. Unlike harmful, it often suggests a serious threat.
malleable: Something malleable can be bent or shaped without breaking. People also use it for people or plans that others can easily change or control. It is similar to flexible, but often suggests too much influence from others.
malnutrition: Malnutrition happens when the body does not get enough of the food or nutrients it needs to stay healthy. It is more than simply missing one meal. The word is common in health reports and talks about poverty.
mammoth: Extremely large in size, scope, effort, or importance. It adds force to something already unusually big and difficult, often making it sound impressive or daunting; huge is a simpler alternative.
man-bites-dog: This describes something so unusual that it turns our normal expectations upside down. It often introduces surprising news in an attention-grabbing, playful way. A dog biting a man is normal, but a man biting a dog is not.
manifold: Existing in many forms, parts, or examples. It sounds polished and formal, so many or various will often fit better in everyday conversation. You may see it in writing about needs, uses, or difficulties.
many-moons-ago: A story that happened long ago can begin with this old-fashioned phrase. The moon cycles through many months, so many moons suggests a long stretch of time. It feels warm and nostalgic, but it is not a good way to give an exact date.
mark-my-word: This is a strong promise that something will happen or that someone is right. It shows confidence and adds emphasis to your words. Unlike a real written promise, it is mainly used to warn or challenge someone.
mark-my-words: Mark my words means remember what I say because I am sure. People use it to make a strong prediction or insist that something will happen. The literal image is writing down someone’s words so they can be checked later.
martinet: A martinet is a person who demands strict rules and harsh obedience. The word is critical because it suggests that the person is too severe. It is stronger and more formal than simply calling someone a disciplinarian.
masticate: To masticate is to chew food carefully until it is easy to swallow. It sounds technical, but people sometimes use it in a funny way. In normal conversation, chew is the natural word.
mastiff: A mastiff is a large, powerful dog, often known for being calm and gentle with its family. Its size can make it look frightening, even when it is friendly. The word can also mean any large dog.
materialism: Materialism means putting possessions, wealth, and physical comfort above other values. In everyday criticism, it suggests that money and things have become too important. In philosophy, it is the belief that only physical matter exists.
matter-of-fact: You add a true detail or correct something with this phrase when the point should be clear. It often sounds calm and helpful, like a teacher adding one important fact. If your tone is sharp, it can feel like a quick correction.
maudlin: This describes sadness that becomes tearful, self-pitying, or overly sentimental. People use it critically, so it is closer to lugubrious than to the quiet sadness of melancholy.
me-too: This is a quick, informal way to say that you share the same feeling, opinion, or experience as someone else. It works well in casual conversations and group chats. In formal situations, explain the shared view more clearly.
mean-business: You show that you are serious and ready to act firmly. People use it to warn others that excuses, delays, or poor performance will not be accepted.
megalomania: Megalomania is an extreme belief that you are more important, powerful, or successful than you really are. In everyday use, it criticizes someone who has become too proud or full of self-importance. It can also refer to a serious mental health condition.
melancholy: This is a deep, quiet sadness that makes someone think about loss or the passing of time. It often appears with words like a feeling of melancholy and sounds more reflective than sudden grief.
memory-lane: This is a journey into memories from earlier times. The lane is a path back into the past, so people use it when old stories, photos, or places bring back feelings. It is often warm, but it can also bring sad memories.
mendacious: A mendacious person is deliberately dishonest and often makes a habit of lying. It is a strong, formal word, so it is stronger and more serious than simply calling someone deceptive.
menial: Menial describes simple, repetitive work that people often consider low in status. The word may sound insulting, especially when used about a person, so care is needed. It is different from difficult work, since the main issue is status and routine.
mess-up: You turn a situation into a mess when you make a mistake or handle something badly. People often say this about a failed plan, damaged result, or confusing mistake. It is more direct and informal than making an error.
metamorphosis: A metamorphosis is a complete change in the form or nature of something. The change often happens gradually, like a caterpillar becoming a butterfly. People also use it for big personal or organisational changes.
meticulous: Careful attention to every small detail is meticulous. It is almost always praise for someone's precise work, while fussy can mean too fussy about small things. It describes careful actions, not a person's general cleverness.
middle-of-nowhere: This describes a place far from towns, shops, and other busy places. The empty space in the middle suggests isolation, so it may sound inconvenient or a little funny. It is common for describing remote countryside.
mien: Mien means the expression and manner that give a person a special impression. It often focuses on the face, body language, or general air, rather than the person’s true character. It is a slightly literary word, so it sounds more formal than manner.
mile-a-minute: This describes someone moving, speaking, or working very fast. The picture is covering a full mile in only one minute, which is far faster than normal. It can also suggest that someone is speaking too quickly to understand.
milieu: A milieu is the set of social, cultural, or work conditions around something. It helps explain how a person, group, or creative work develops. In everyday speech, environment or background is often easier to use.
mind-you: Mind you adds a qualification or important point to something you have just said. It sounds like that said or but remember, and it is common in British and Irish English. It helps the speaker correct or balance an earlier thought.
miscreant: A miscreant is a wicked, dishonest, or shameful person. The word shows strong disapproval and sounds old-fashioned or dramatic, so it is more common in crime stories and formal writing. A common phrase is notorious miscreant.
mission-accomplished: This says that a goal or task has been successfully finished. It can sound proud and satisfied, but people also use it jokingly when the result feels too easy or incomplete. It comes from the idea of completing an assigned mission.
mitigate: Making a bad situation less harmful or painful is to mitigate it. The word sounds calm and responsible. It does not remove the problem; it shows that you are reducing its effects.
mixed-bag: A mixed bag contains different kinds of things, just as an outcome can have good and bad parts. People use it when there is no single clear result and many details are mixed together. It is similar to saying a mixture.
modest: Being modest means you do not show off your skills, power, or success more than you should. It can also describe something fairly small, such as a modest home or income, and it often goes with the words gain, amount, and income.
modify: To modify something is to change it a little to make it better, clearer, or more suitable. This is a smaller change than replacing it completely. It is common with plans, documents, designs, and computer settings.
mollify: To mollify someone is to calm their anger or reduce the tension between people. It often involves gentle words, kindness, or compromise, and it is similar to soothe but sounds more formal.
moment-of-truth: A moment of truth is when the truth becomes clear or you must make an important choice. The situation may feel tense after a long wait. People use it for a revealing talk, a hard test, or a decision that cannot be avoided.
monolithic: Made as one solid, unified whole, like a single block. Figuratively, it describes an organization or system that seems impossible to change or influence, and it often carries a critical tone.
more-than-meets-the-eye: There may be more to a person or situation than you can see at first. People use this phrase when the obvious facts do not tell the whole story, often suggesting that something is hidden or more complicated than it appears.
moribund: Something moribund still exists, but it has little energy, purpose, or power to continue. People often use it for old organisations, systems, or ideas. It is similar to dying, but it can also mean mainly becoming ineffective.
mortality: Mortality is the fact that all living things will eventually die. It can also mean the number of deaths in a group during a certain time. The word often appears in serious writing about life, death, or public health.
mortify: To mortify someone is to make them feel deeply ashamed or embarrassed. It is stronger than ordinary embarrassment, and the common word mortified often describes how someone feels after a serious mistake.
motivate: To motivate someone is to give them a reason to act, try, or keep going. A person may be motivated by money, a goal, encouragement, or personal values, so it is close to encourage but stronger.
move-the-needle: Move the needle means to make a clear, measurable difference to a result. It often appears in business talk, especially in the negative, when a small effort is said not to move the needle. It sounds data-driven, but a number makes it more exact.
much-ado-about-nothing: People make a lot of noise and effort over something small or not worth it. It often shows needless drama, like arguing loudly when no real problem exists. Use it carefully when the issue truly matters to someone else.
mums-the-word: This is a playful way to say that you will keep a secret. It can promise silence, but it may also mean that someone is deliberately refusing to share what they know. The old picture is simple: mum means stay quiet, and the word is the secret.
mundane: Something mundane is ordinary and happens all the time, with little excitement or interest. The word can sound dismissive when people describe dull work, conversations, or events. It helps show that something lacks the special quality of a memorable experience.
munificent: Munificent means unusually generous, especially with money, gifts, or support. It sounds formal and admiring, often suggesting that the gift was large or important. It is stronger than generous and is common in formal writing.
murky: Murky describes water, skies, or situations where the details are hard to see or understand. It often suggests that something is both dim and confusing, so do not confuse it with simply being dirty.
myriad: A very large number of people, things, examples, or problems. It sounds polished and literary rather than natural in speech, so countless or many usually works better in conversation instead.
nadir: The lowest or worst point in a person's life, career, health, or chances. It is stronger and more literary than low point, and people often use it when things have reached their worst.
nail-in-ones-coffin: A nail in someone’s coffin helps bring about their downfall, often as one problem among several. The image is literal: a nail secures a coffin and is connected with death. People use this phrase for serious actions or events that push a person or plan toward failure.
naive: Naive describes someone who lacks experience or careful judgment about how things really work. It can sound innocent, but it may also mean that the person is too easily fooled. People sometimes confuse it with innocent, which does not always suggest poor judgment.
nascent: A nascent thing is new and only beginning to grow or develop. It may have the potential to become important later. The word describes an early stage, not something fully established or successful yet.
nature-calls: People say this when they badly need to use the toilet, especially if they do not want to talk about it directly. It can also be a joke about wanting to spend time outdoors, because nature is calling you.
nebulous: A nebulous idea, plan, or boundary is vague and hard to define. It is not simply unknown; the details are there but cannot be seen clearly. The word sounds more formal than vague, but it carries the same basic idea.
neck-and-neck: Two competitors are so close that neither one is clearly ahead. It also describes two things that are almost equal, such as prices or scores. The image is of horses running side by side with their heads at the same level.
nefarious: A nefarious action is clearly evil, harmful, or intentionally wrong. People use it for serious wrongdoing, especially hidden acts, but it can sound too dramatic for a small mistake.
negligent: Negligent means failing to give proper care to something that is your responsibility. It often carries blame because the mistake could have been avoided. It is more formal and serious than careless, which can describe a less important mistake.
negligible: Something negligible is so small that it does not change the result. People use this in reports or careful estimates, but it may sound too technical in normal conversation. It is similar to tiny, but it also suggests that something does not matter.
neophyte: A neophyte is someone who is new to a field, activity, or group. The word can sound a little formal and may seem patronising if an experienced person is called one. Beginner is a more common and friendly word.
nepotism: Nepotism means giving jobs, benefits, or chances to relatives because of your family connection. People usually use it critically, because it is unfair to those without relatives in important places. It is often discussed with words like jobs, favouritism, and relatives.
neurotic: Neurotic describes someone who seems extremely anxious, tense, or easily upset. The word can be insulting because it suggests that the reactions are excessive or hard to control. Its older medical meaning is now outdated, so it is best used in everyday criticism.
neutralize: To neutralize something is to make it harmless or stop it from causing conflict. This may involve removing a danger, cancelling an effect, or reducing opposition. It sounds firm and controlled, rather than friendly or gentle.
never-a-dull-moment: A situation keeps being lively, busy, or entertaining, with no quiet or boring time. People often use it after a fun or exciting event, though it can also mean things were hectic and tiring.
new-year-new-me: This is a playful way to say that a new year is the chance to change and improve yourself. People often use it in holiday posts or messages, even when their plans are not very serious.
nirvana: Nirvana means perfect peace, often with no worry or pain. In everyday English, people use it for complete happiness, sometimes in a dreamy or joking way, while its Buddhist meaning involves freedom from desire and suffering.
no-big-deal: You say this when a problem is small and does not need much worry. It is casual and friendly, like telling someone to relax. However, if they are truly upset, it can sound as if you are dismissing their feelings.
no-contest: One choice is clearly better, so there is no point in arguing or comparing. People also use it when everyone simply agrees, often in a relaxed or slightly joking way.
no-cure-no-pay: This payment arrangement means the client does not have to pay unless the promised result happens. It is common in health care, but the exact rules still matter, so it is not always a full guarantee. Ask what counts as success and who decides.
no-deal: You are firmly refusing an offer or saying that a plan will not work. It sounds final in business talks, but in everyday talk it can simply mean an idea has been rejected.
no-dice: Something did not work, or a request was refused. This sounds informal and a little sharp, so it is better with friends than in a formal workplace. It comes from a bad throw of the dice, meaning an unlucky result.
no-entry: This tells people that they cannot go into a particular place or area. It is common on signs, and sometimes only workers or other approved people may enter.
no-fixed-abode: This describes someone who does not have a permanent home or address. It sounds formal and is more common in serious writing than in everyday conversation.
no-flies-on: Someone is very smart and careful, so they are hard to trick. It can also mean that something looks honest and has no hidden problems. The phrase is now a little old-fashioned and often describes a smart, careful person.
no-free-lunch: Every good offer has a catch, so you often must accept a limit or give something up. People say this when an offer seems too good to be true. The old picture is a cheap buffet lunch where each customer could take only one meal.
no-further-action: This tells people that a matter is finished and nobody needs to do anything more. It is common in professional updates, service messages, and reports, and sounds more final than a simple statement that it is done.
no-glove-no-love: This says that you need to make an effort before you can expect support, success, or affection. The glove comes from sports, where players need protection to play safely.
no-hard-feelings: You say this after an argument, mistake, or criticism to show that you are not angry. It is usually friendly and formal enough for serious situations. Among close friends, a shorter phrase like no worries may sound more natural.
no-harm-done: This reassures someone that a mistake or accident did not cause damage or lasting problems. People also use it to accept an apology in a kind and relaxed way.
no-matter-what: This emphasizes that you will do something whatever happens. It can show strong determination, or reassure someone that you will accept any outcome without blaming them.
no-need: Something is unnecessary, so you do not have to do it. This can be a polite way to turn down an offer or tell someone they may relax. With a firmer tone, it can also mean that an action is pointless.
no-offence: You are saying that your honest comment is not meant as an insult. It can soften a difficult point, but it does not stop the other person from feeling hurt or offended.
no-offense: This softens a comment that may hurt or offend someone. It tells the other person that you did not mean to upset them, but it does not make every comment acceptable. Listen to how they react.
no-parking: This tells drivers that they must not leave their vehicle in a particular place. It is usually shown on signs or included in parking rules, and can sound quite direct.
no-picnic: This describes something that is difficult, tiring, or more troublesome than it first seems. People often use it at work or with friends to add some light humor to a complaint.
no-plan-survives-contact-with-the-enemy: Real problems can make even a careful plan fail. People use this saying when unexpected events or strong opposition change the situation. It is serious and slightly dramatic, so it may feel too strong for everyday talk.
no-pressure: This reassures someone that they do not have to act or meet an expectation. It often sounds kind and relaxed when someone needs time to decide. Sometimes it can also mean that you are not forcing them, but you still expect them to act.
no-probs: No probs is a friendly way to say that everything is fine or that you are happy to help. People use it in casual conversations with friends or colleagues they know well, but it is too informal for most work emails.
no-pun-intended: You are saying that a joke was accidental and you were actually being serious. It can also warn listeners that you are about to speak in a completely serious way. People often use it with a playful tone after making a word joke.
no-question: You are very sure about something, with no doubt at all. People use it for facts, clear choices, or points that everyone already agrees on. Adding about it after it makes a direct answer sound more natural.
no-rights-reserved: This label suggests that a creator may allow other people to copy, share, or change the work. It has an open and informal feel, but its legal meaning is not clear without specific permission terms, so it is not the same as public domain.
no-shot: There is almost no chance that something will happen. It sounds blunt and informal, and may mean the event is unlikely or will not happen at all. It is more natural in conversation with people you know well.
no-smoking: No smoking tells people that they cannot smoke in that place. You often see it on signs in offices, restaurants, stations, and other public spaces. It is a clear rule, not a polite request, and breaking it may lead to a fine.
no-soap: You are saying that there is no chance or no possible deal. The sound is blunt and dismissive, so it suits casual talks between people who know each other well. The old picture is someone asking for soap and being told none is available.
no-sooner-said-than-done: This describes something being finished almost as soon as it was requested or mentioned. The literal picture is an action happening before the speaker has even finished talking. It often adds humor, but it can sound slightly old-fashioned.
no-soup-for-you: You will not get what you want because you missed your chance or did not meet the rules. This is a playful, dramatic refusal, often used as teasing among friends. In a serious workplace, it may sound too harsh.
no-string-attached: This offer has no extra conditions or duties attached to it. The old image comes from a puppet, which is controlled by strings; without strings, it can move freely. People use it for gifts, jobs, and deals, but they should check the full terms.
no-strings-attached: This describes a gift, deal, or offer with nothing extra attached. The picture is of a package tied with a string that would hold it back; here, no string means no hidden condition. Informal adverts may still hide important details in the small print.
no-thanks-to: Something bad happened because of the person or thing named after it. The words usually sound like the opposite of thanks, so they often carry humor or blame. Use them carefully because they can sound sharp.
no-time-to-lose: You need to act right away because waiting could cost you a chance. People use this for deadlines or fast-changing situations, but it can sound overly dramatic when nothing is really urgent.
no-trespassing: No trespassing warns people not to enter private or restricted land. It usually appears on signs near gates, fences, or buildings. The exact legal power of this warning depends on local law, so follow any extra instructions from the owner.
no-win-no-fee: A lawyer agrees to charge nothing unless the case is won. People use this for injury, debt, and compensation claims, but clients may still need to pay court or expert costs, so check the terms first.
no-word-of-a-lie: Every word is true, with no lie mixed in. People use this when confirming a surprising fact or telling what really happened. It is stronger than simply saying something is true.
nobodys-perfect: Everyone has mistakes and qualities that others may dislike, so nobody is truly perfect. People use this phrase to show understanding or forgiveness. It can reassure someone who feels bad, but it may sound too casual for a serious complaint.
noisome: A noisome smell, sound, or situation is so unpleasant that people want to avoid it. It is stronger and more literary than the word bad, and it is often used for smells that are especially offensive.
nomadic: Nomadic describes people who move from place to place instead of staying in one home. It can describe a whole community, a way of life, or workers who travel often. It may sound romantic or free, but it can also suggest a lack of stable housing.
nominal: A nominal role, value, or power exists in name or as a label, but has little real effect. It may describe an official title with no real authority or a figure used only as a starting point. It can sound neutral, but it often hints that something is mostly symbolic.
nondescript: Something that is nondescript looks ordinary and has no special features that people notice. People use it for buildings, clothes, or places that blend into their surroundings; it is close to bland but is less negative.
none-of-your-beeswax: You are telling someone that the matter is none of their business and they should not interfere. It can be playful between friends, but at work a softer line is safer. The old picture imagines your affairs sealed under your own wax.
none-other-than: This points to one exact person or thing, often when the choice is surprising or special. It adds emphasis and can sound admiring or dramatic. Do not use it in every situation, because it may feel too grand.
nonentity: A nonentity is a person or thing with very little power, importance, or influence. The word can sound insulting when someone is ignored or treated as unimportant. It is often used in the phrase political nonentity.
nostalgia: Nostalgia is a warm wish to return to happy or meaningful times in the past. It can feel affectionate, but also sad because those times cannot come back. People often use it for old memories, songs, or childhood.
not-a-patch-on: This compares someone or something with a weaker, patched version of itself. It means they are far less impressive, skilled or useful than the other choice. The image of an old patch suggests something worn and less valuable than the original.
not-an-option: If something is not an option, it is impossible or not allowed in the situation. People use this firm phrase to close off a choice, often by saying what can happen instead. It can sound blunt, so explain your reason.
not-before-time: Something is happening at the right or expected time, not too early. People say this to calm someone who is worried about waiting. It does not mean the event is late.
not-feeling-it: You are not interested, excited, or convinced about something right now. It can honestly show a lack of motivation or connection. If you mean you disagree, it is better to give a clear reason rather than only saying this.
not-for-nothing: You use this when you are about to make a point or give advice that has a good reason behind it. It is like saying, “I am not saying this just to cause trouble”; it can sound a little defensive if used often.
not-much: Not much means a small amount or less than people expected. Depending on the sentence, it can describe effort, progress, time, or impact. It often sounds calm and understated rather than strongly negative, such as when you say there was not much rain.
not-necessarily: This softens a statement and shows that it may be true, but it is not certain or always the case. It can prevent a disagreement from becoming too strong. It may also mean that something might not be true.
not-on-any-account: You absolutely will not do or allow something to happen. This gives a firm refusal and leaves no room for doubt. It is a little formal, so an ordinary no often works better in casual talk.
not-ones-first-rodeo: You have done this before, so you know what to expect and do not find it hard. It comes from rodeos, where returning riders are familiar with the event, but today people use it to show confidence or dismiss a task as easy.
not-saying-much: You speak only a little because you are quiet or have little to add. It can simply describe a reserved person, but at work it may suggest that you are holding back an opinion. It is different from having nothing at all to say.
not-so-fast: Wait a moment and do not jump ahead too quickly. People use this to stop an assumption, a plan, or an argument before it goes further. It can sound playful, but rude if the speaker does not explain the pause.
not-the-best-use-of-our-time: You are saying a task or discussion may not be worth the time it will take. It focuses on priorities rather than saying you dislike the task. It can sound dismissive if the task matters to someone else.
not-the-brightest-bulb-in-the-chandelier: The person is not very smart or quick to understand things. The image compares them to a dim light bulb on a bright chandelier. It is funny but insulting, so use it only with close friends and in a relaxed mood.
not-the-end-of-the-world: The problem is serious, but it will not destroy everything or cause lasting harm. People use this to comfort someone who is upset or apologizing. It can sound unhelpful if the person still needs real support.
not-the-sharpest-crayon-in-the-box: The person is not very smart and may be slow to understand. A blunt crayon cannot write as well as a sharp one, so the image compares them with the cleverest person in the group. It is playful but can be rude.
not-the-sharpest-pencil-in-the-box: The person is not very smart, quick to understand, or good at making decisions. A dull pencil writes less well than a sharp one, so the image points to the least clever person. It is light teasing, but still insulting.
not-the-sharpest-tool-in-the-box: This is a teasing way to say that someone is not very smart or quick to understand. It comes from the image of a dull tool among sharp ones. Use it only with people you know well, because it can sound insulting.
not-the-sharpest-tool-in-the-shed: This is a light, teasing way to call someone not very clever. The image is of a tool in a shed that is duller than the others. It is similar to the box version, but can sound more insulting, so keep it among friends.
not-to-be-outdone: Doing well enough to match someone else is often not enough; this phrase says you try to do just as well or better. People use it after another person or group achieves something. It often shows friendly rivalry rather than anger.
not-to-brag: This makes a success sound modest before you tell it. People often use it in a friendly or playful way when they are clearly pleased. It is common after good news, but it can sound false if you are seeking attention.
not-to-worry: You tell someone not to feel worried because the situation is under control or not serious. It is warm and casual, often used after someone mentions a problem. First show that you understand their concern, or it may sound careless.
not-your-fathers: This compares something with an old-fashioned idea or way of doing things. It can be playful and funny among friends when the contrast is clear. However, it may sound rude when used about colleagues, older people, or a serious issue.
nothing-about-us-without-us: People who will be affected by a decision should help make that decision. It is used when asking for real participation, not just telling people about choices later. The literal idea is that nothing involving us should happen without us.
nothing-short-of: This gives strong emphasis to something that is completely impressive, unexpected, or extreme. You usually put it before a noun, such as a success or a disaster. It is stronger than simply saying very, so use it carefully.
nothing-to-it: This says a task is easy and needs little effort. People use it to reassure others or praise them for doing something well. Be careful, because it can sound like you are dismissing a real difficulty.
now-hear-this: Use this when you want someone to stop talking and listen to your important point. It can be playful with friends, but it may sound bossy at work. It is more direct and forceful than just saying listen carefully.
now-thats-what-i-call: This shows strong approval for something you think is exactly right. People often use it with a bit of excitement when a choice or result surprises them. It is more casual and dramatic than simply saying good job.
now-were-talking: This shows that you finally understand, agree with or feel excited about an idea. It sounds friendly and relieved, as if the conversation has reached the right point. It is informal and usually fits social or work conversations.
now-what: A situation is unclear or unfinished, so you are asking what should happen next. The words may show uncertainty, frustration, or a wish for direction. Among friends, they can simply be a relaxed way to ask for the next step.
now-youre-cooking: This says that someone has found the right way to do something and is doing it well. The cooking image suggests that the food will turn out well because the person now knows what to do. It is friendly and encouraging.
now-youre-talking: You say this when an idea or comment is sensible and matches what you think. It sounds pleased and approving, like now you're cooking. It is less precise than saying exactly what you like about the idea.
nuance: A small difference in meaning, feeling, tone, or color is a nuance. Saying a topic needs nuance means it is more complicated than it first appears. Unlike a detail, a nuance is a subtle change that changes how something feels.
nuanced: A nuanced view notices small differences instead of dividing things into simple groups. People use it for careful opinions, feelings, or details, especially at work. It can sound vague if you do not explain the differences.
nullify: To nullify something is to make it invalid or remove its effect. It often appears in legal or formal contexts, such as cancelling a decision, and is stronger than simply canceling a plan.
nurture: Nurture means helping someone or something grow through care, support, and encouragement over time. It is often used for children, plants, skills, ideas, and relationships. It is commonly confused with nature, as in nature versus nurture.
nutritive: Food or substances that give your body what it needs to grow and stay well. The word is often used in food science and health, but it does not mean the food is healthy in every way.
nuts-and-bolts: These are the basic practical details of a subject or task. You use the phrase when discussing how something really works or what must be done, not its wider ideas.
obliterate: To obliterate something is to destroy it completely or remove every trace of it. People use it for buildings, records, evidence, or even whole groups in very strong writing. It is more dramatic than destroy, because nothing is left.
obloquy: Strong public blame is called obloquy. It is a formal, forceful word and can damage the person’s reputation as well as their character. People often use it with the expression draw obloquy upon someone.
obsequious: Obsequious describes someone who tries too hard to please, flatter, or obey another person. It often suggests that the politeness is fake or done to gain favor. It is more critical than respectful, which may be sincere and natural.
obsess: To obsess over something means to think about it again and again, even when you cannot stop. The thought may take up more attention than it deserves. It can be harmless, like a new hobby, or linked to anxiety.
obsolescence: Obsolescence is the process of becoming old-fashioned and no longer useful. It often happens when newer products, technology, or methods replace older ones. It can also describe skills that are becoming less valuable.
obviate: To obviate a problem is to remove it before it causes trouble. It often appears with concern, risk, or difficulty in formal writing. Unlike avoid, it means dealing with the obstacle itself, not just keeping away from it.
octogenarian: An octogenarian is someone who is 80 to 89 years old. It is a neutral and exact label, often used in news or research about age groups. It is more precise than the general phrase elderly person.
odious: Odious describes something deeply unpleasant or hateful. It is stronger and more formal than annoying, so people often use it for cruel behaviour or offensive acts. A truly odious person causes strong dislike in others.
off-the-scale: When something is off the scale, it is extremely high, large, or much bigger than normal. It often describes prices, demand, growth, or unusual levels. The picture comes from going past the highest mark on a measuring scale, so it feels more informal and vivid than saying enormous or record-breaking.
ominous: Ominous describes a sign or feeling that something bad may happen soon. It creates tension, but it does not prove that danger is real. One common partner is an ominous silence.
omnipotent: An omnipotent person, god, or system has unlimited power and can do anything. The word is often used for fictional rulers or perfect control. In criticism, it can mean one person has too much power over everyone else.
omnivorous: Animals that eat both plants and animals are omnivorous, and people can also use the word for eating many kinds of food. It may also describe someone interested in many subjects, often in a playful way.
on-all-fours: On all fours can describe someone on their hands and knees, or making a determined effort to achieve something difficult. The literal picture of crawling helps explain the idea of going to great lengths. People also use it to suggest a search for something.
on-deaths-doorstep: Death seems extremely close, and something bad may happen at any moment. The image comes from standing right outside a dead person’s door, so it is stronger and more dramatic than simply saying someone is in danger.
on-the-brink: You are very close to a serious point, such as a crisis or a big change. The image is someone standing at the edge of a cliff, where one small step could be dangerous. People use it to show that action is urgent, often with of, as in on the brink of collapse.
on-the-edge-of-ones-seat: Feeling unable to sit still because you are excited, worried, or waiting for something important means you are on the edge of your seat. It often describes following a tense event closely. The literal image is sitting so forward that you might fall off.
on-the-fence: To be undecided between two choices or unwilling to support either side. It can sound negative when someone avoids making a choice. The picture is sitting on a fence between two fields.
on-the-fly: Doing something on the fly means doing it quickly as a situation happens, without preparing first. The image comes from acting while in the air. People often use it at work when a problem needs a fast solution, and it may show that you were unprepared.
on-the-front-burner: Something is being handled with high priority right now. It suggests a task needs attention soon, often a current project or problem, but not necessarily the most important long-term goal.
on-the-go: You are on the go when you are busy, moving between places, or switching from one task to another. It often describes a hectic day with little time to rest. It can also mean you are out and about.
on-the-other-hand: On the other hand introduces a different or opposite side of an idea. It helps a speaker make a fair comparison by showing another possibility. People often use it in conversations and written arguments, especially after presenting one clear point.
on-the-radar: Something is on the radar when people notice it or start to think about it. The picture comes from an object appearing on a radar screen. It may be watched closely, but it does not mean action will happen soon.
on-the-receiving-end: Someone is on the receiving end when criticism, blame, or bad results come to them. The image is of standing at the end of a line where blows or messages arrive. It is not about receiving something good; the person is getting the unwanted side.
on-the-same-page: On the same page means people agree or understand a plan in the same way. Teams often use it before starting work to check that everyone understands the goal. It is similar to being in agreement, but focuses on shared understanding.
on-the-spot: On the spot can mean doing something immediately, without waiting. It can also mean at the exact place where something is happening, such as a decision made where you stand. The phrase often feels direct and urgent.
on-the-verge: Something important is very close to happening, but it has not happened yet. People use it to build tension, often followed by “of” and an action, such as quitting, laughing, or falling.
on-thin-ice: On thin ice means you are in a risky situation where one mistake could cause serious trouble. The picture is walking on ice that may break, and people use it for both physical danger and problems at work or with other people.
on-your-mark-get-set-go: Get ready and start now. It has an energetic, exciting feeling and is common in races, games, and group activities, though people also use it playfully when starting a task.
once-a-thief-always-a-thief: Someone who has cheated before may be expected to cheat again. It suggests that people keep their basic habits, but it can sound unfair and judgmental because one past act does not always decide the future.
once-bitten-twice-shy: A bad experience can make you careful the next time you face something similar. The animal picture explains it: after one bite, it runs when another creature appears. People use it with a slightly rueful tone.
once-in-a-blue-moon: Once in a blue moon means something happens very rarely. It is a light way to say that something almost never happens, but still can happen sometimes. The unusual blue moon gives the rare event a playful feeling.
one-bad-apple: One person can harm a whole group or spoil an otherwise good situation. The image is a rotten apple making nearby apples rot, but the phrase can be harsh because it blames one person instead of the real problem.
one-could-hear-a-pin-drop: The room is so quiet that even the smallest sound would be clear. People use it when everyone stops talking and listens carefully, often after asking for silence. It can sound a little old-fashioned.
one-for-all-all-for-one: Each person supports the group, and the group supports each person. People use it to show shared responsibility and loyalty, often as a team motto. It is stronger than simply agreeing to work together.
one-of-us: The person belongs to the same group, team, or community as the speaker. It can show warm support, or it can mean everyone should share responsibility for the task. It sounds inclusive rather than formal or distant.
one-strike-and-youre-out: Make one serious mistake and you lose your chance to continue. The words come from baseball, where three strikes mean a batter is out, but here one strike is enough. It can also be used playfully.
one-thing-leads-to-another: Events can start a chain that leads to another event, and this phrase describes that chain. It is often used when the final result is unexpected, funny, or awkward, so the speaker may not explain every cause.
ones-bark-is-worse-than-ones-bite: Someone’s harsh words or threats are more serious than their real actions. People use it when a person complains loudly but is unlikely to carry out the threat, so it should not be used when the danger is real.
ones-blood-runs-cold: A frightening or shocking moment can make you feel suddenly afraid. The image is that fear makes your blood feel cold, like ice. In everyday speech, people often say “my blood ran cold.”
ones-days-are-numbered: Someone has only a short time left before something bad happens. It can be completely serious or exaggerated to show that a person is in serious trouble. The image comes from counting down the final days of someone’s life.
ones-gotta-do-what-ones-gotta-do: A person must accept a duty and do it, even when it is hard or unwanted. The wording shows resignation and a little frustration, so it fits personal problems better than serious formal writing.
ones-heart-out: You show your deepest feelings fully, without hiding any of them. The picture is taking your heart out and holding it open for others to see. People use it for honest speech, music, or creative work, but it can sound overly dramatic in everyday situations.
ones-race-is-run: A person’s active career or useful time has ended. The image comes from finishing a race, so the feeling is serious and final. It is stronger and more emotional than simply saying someone has retired.
only-time-will-tell: The truth or result is not clear yet, but it may become clear later. People use this when a situation is still uncertain and waiting is the only way to find out. It can also be used in a joking way.
opportunity-knocks: A good chance becomes available to you. The image is someone knocking at your door with a useful offer or opening. People use it for jobs, invitations, and new contacts, and it often suggests you should notice the chance and act.
opprobrium: Public disgrace and severe criticism that damage a person’s name are called opprobrium. It sounds formal and is often used in writing about scandals or serious moral faults. It is similar to obloquy but focuses more on shame than blame.
opulence: Opulence means great wealth, comfort, and luxury. It often describes rich homes, fine possessions, or an extravagant way of living. It can sound admiring, but it may also suggest that the luxury is excessive.
ordinary: Something ordinary is normal and not special. People use it for everyday things, but it can also sound a little insulting when it describes a person or their ideas as if they lack interest or excitement.
originate: To originate means to begin or come into existence. A person, group, place, or idea may originate it, and it may also develop from a particular source. People often use it to talk about where plans or movements started.
ornate: Ornate describes something decorated with many rich or detailed designs. People use it for buildings, furniture, clothes, or fancy writing. It can praise the beauty, but it may also suggest that the decoration is more important than use.
ostensible: An ostensible reason is the reason people give when the real purpose may be different. It sounds careful and slightly doubtful, and it often goes with words like purpose, reason, or claim.
ostentatious: Someone who is ostentatious wants attention through bright clothes, expensive things, or an exaggerated display. The word is usually negative and suggests that status or wealth is being put on show. It can describe a dramatic entrance meant to impress people.
oust: To oust someone is to force them out of a job, group, position, or place. It often suggests that power, competition, or pressure caused the removal. Oust is more forceful and final than simply leave or remove.
out-of-nowhere: Something happens out of nowhere when it appears suddenly, without warning or an obvious reason. The image is of something coming from a place that was not there before. People use it for news, ideas, visitors, or surprises.
out-of-the-blue: Something can happen suddenly, with no warning at all. It appears like an object arriving in an open blue sky. People use it for surprising news, visits, problems, or decisions; the surprise itself does not have to be bad.
out-on-a-limb: This describes taking a risky position where you may face criticism or failure. It often suggests going against the safer or more popular choice. The picture of someone balancing on a narrow branch shows how exposed they are.
outgoing: An outgoing person is friendly, talkative, and comfortable with others. People often use it for someone’s social manner at work or in a new group. It can also mean leaving or being sent away, so the context matters.
overt: Overt actions, feelings, or attitudes are open and easy for others to notice. It is the opposite of hidden or secret, but it does not mean that the action was extreme.
palliate: To make pain or a serious problem less bad, but not to remove its cause. Doctors may use it when treating symptoms, while governments may use it when reducing a difficult problem without solving it fully.
paltry: Paltry describes an amount that is too small or poor to be enough. It often describes money, effort, support, or results, and it shows that the speaker is disappointed. It is stronger and more critical than simply saying small.
panacea: A panacea is claimed to solve a problem completely, often several problems at once. It sounds hopeful but can sound skeptical, like this cannot fix everything. People use it for cures, methods, or ideas that seem too good to be simple.
pandemonium: Pandemonium describes a wild, noisy, and confused scene that is hard to control. The word can describe either great excitement or complete disorder. It sounds strong and dramatic, so it is common in news reports and storytelling.
pandoras-box: Opening one problem can release a crowd of new ones. In the old story, Pandora opens a box and lets every trouble escape, so the trouble cannot be put back. People use it when one action causes many wider problems.
pants-on-fire: A statement is such an obvious lie that the speaker seems to be in danger of being caught. The picture of burning pants shows panic and shame. It is more dramatic and emphatic than simply calling someone a liar.
parable: A parable is a short story that teaches a lesson, often about right and wrong. People use it when a simple example makes a big idea easier to remember. It is like an analogy, but usually tells a story.
paradox: A paradox seems to say two opposite things at once, but the deeper point connects them. It makes you question your first idea and see a situation in a new way. It is more than just a confusing contradiction.
paragon: A person or thing that is admired as a perfect model is a paragon. It is strong praise but sounds quite grand and literary, so it may seem unusual in daily conversation. It often goes with of a quality such as honesty or kindness.
paramount: Paramount means more important than anything else in a particular situation. It has a strong, official tone and is common in work and legal writing. It is similar to essential, but it stresses the highest priority.
paroxysm: A paroxysm is a sudden, intense burst of emotion, pain, or movement. It rises quickly, reaches its strongest point, and then passes. The word sounds more dramatic and formal than an ordinary outburst.
parsimonious: A parsimonious person spends as little money or uses as few resources as possible. It often suggests someone is stingy, but it can be positive when it means using limited resources well.
pass-away: This is a careful and indirect way to say that someone has died. It sounds softer and more respectful, especially in news reports and speeches. In everyday conversation, it can feel distant when speaking about a loved one.
pass-up: You refuse or reject an opportunity, offer, or chance. It suggests a deliberate choice, even when the opportunity was useful, such as passing up a good job offer or a chance to travel.
pathetic: Calling something pathetic says it is weak, disappointing, and almost deserves ridicule. Today it is usually a harsh insult rather than a sign of sympathy. It can sound dramatic or exaggerated, so use it carefully when speaking directly to people.
pathological: This describes a disease or an abnormal condition in the body. In everyday use, it can also describe behaviour that is extreme, obsessive or far out of proportion to ordinary life.
patient: A patient person stays calm and waits without giving up. It is usually praise, especially when someone faces a slow or difficult situation, but it can also mean they are simply putting up with a problem.
patriarch: A patriarch is a respected man who leads a family, organisation, or tradition. It can also suggest old-fashioned male authority. Patriarch is often confused with matriarch, which refers to a leading woman.
paucity: A paucity means a small supply or a lack of something. It is a formal word often used for time, money, information, or chances. It is close to scarcity, but it often focuses on having too little of a needed thing.
pave-the-way: Paving the way means preparing the path so something else can happen more easily. The literal image is workers making a smooth road before others travel on it. People use it for practical steps, social changes, or support that leads to a later result.
pay-attention: To pay attention means to listen, watch, or think carefully so you do not miss what is happening. People use it as a common instruction to focus. It can also suggest that someone was not paying enough attention before.
pecuniary: Pecuniary means connected with money or financial value. It is common in legal, business, and academic writing about payments, losses, or benefits. It sounds more formal than simply saying financial.
pedagogue: A pedagogue is a teacher who is known for a careful and principled way of teaching. It sounds more formal than teacher and may also suggest someone who is strict about methods. Another accepted spelling is pedagogue.
pedal-to-the-metal: Someone is pushing harder and moving faster, often with sudden energy. The image comes from pressing a car pedal all the way down. It suggests urgency and excitement, rather than careful or steady progress.
pedantic: A pedantic person pays too much attention to exact words, rules, or tiny details. It often sounds critical, like the person is being fussy, though it can sometimes praise careful accuracy.
penance: Penance is something you do to make up for a mistake or show deep regret. It may involve giving up something or doing a hard task. It often carries a serious moral or religious sense, so it can sound old-fashioned.
penchant: A penchant is a strong natural liking for something. People often have one for a subject, style, or type of food. It is a slightly formal word for preference and can shape what they choose.
penitent: A penitent person feels deep sorrow about wrongdoing and wants to make amends. The word shows a serious change in attitude, not just a quick apology. It can also be used as a noun for such a person.
pensive: Pensive means quietly thinking about something, often with a little sadness or uncertainty. The person is not simply resting or waiting; they are turning something over in their mind. Pensive has a softer, sadder mood than thoughtful.
penury: Penury means extreme poverty or a serious lack of basic needs. It sounds strong and formal, so it is more common in serious writing than everyday speech. It can also mean a very poor supply of something useful.
perceive: To perceive something is to notice it and form an idea about what it means. People use it when they are observing, judging, or interpreting a situation. Your idea may be right, but perceiving does not make it true.
perceptive: A perceptive person notices small details and understands what people mean or feel. It is a compliment about good listening and judgement. A perceptive comment points to something important that others may have missed.
peregrination: A long journey with several stops, often with some uncertainty along the way. The word carries a sense of exploration and wandering, but people sometimes use it jokingly for a simple trip across town.
peremptory: A peremptory decision, tone, or command is final and leaves no room for discussion. It can also suggest impatience or an unwillingness to hear other views. People use it for orders that feel rigid, firm, and sometimes unfair.
perfect-storm: Several hard problems can come together and make a bad situation worse. The storm picture comes from different weather forces joining to create one powerful storm. People use it for serious difficulties, not small annoyances.
perfidious: A perfidious person pretends to be loyal while secretly planning to betray someone. The word suggests a careful, hidden act of deceit, so it is stronger and more dramatic than just calling someone unreliable.
perfunctory: Something done in a perfunctory way is only done as a routine, with little care or real interest. It often criticizes someone for going through the motions, especially at work.
permeate: Permeate means to spread through a material, place, group, or set of ideas. The spread is often slow and may reach everywhere. It is often confused with penetrate, which means to pass into or through something.
pernicious: Something pernicious causes serious harm in a slow or hidden way. People often use it for bad habits, influences, or ideas whose damage is not obvious at first.
perpetrate: Carrying out a crime or another very wrong act is to perpetrate it. It is a strong, formal word often used in legal reports and serious news stories, not ordinary talk. Do not confuse it with pursue, which means to follow or seek something.
perpetuate: To perpetuate something is to keep it going, often for a long time. People use it for beliefs, traditions, problems, or unfair systems that continue because of certain actions. It highlights the cause of the continuing situation.
persevere: To persevere means to keep trying even when a task is slow, hard, or full of setbacks. It highlights steady effort and learning from mistakes, so it often sounds encouraging, though it is a formal word.
persevering: A persevering person keeps working toward a goal despite delays or repeated problems. It is usually a positive word for determination, but it can sound negative if the person is refusing to change a bad course.
persistent: A persistent effort continues despite difficulty or interruption. It can show strong determination, but it can also mean someone keeps pushing in a way others see as stubborn or will not let the issue go.
perspicacious: A perspicacious person has a sharp mind and quickly sees what is really going on. It is a strong compliment for insight and clear thinking, not just being clever. People use it when someone notices hidden meanings or sees through a trick.
persuasive: Persuasive means able to make someone believe or do something by giving clear, strong reasons. We call an argument, speech, or presentation persuasive when it changes the listener’s view. It can also describe a person whose manner makes others want to listen.
pertinent: Pertinent information is directly connected to the issue being discussed. It sounds thoughtful and professional when you point out something that matters. It can also sound firm or slightly stern when used to reject an unrelated question.
peruse: To peruse a document is to read or examine it carefully, usually to understand or judge it. It sounds more formal than look over and suggests that you will notice important details. People often use it about contracts, reports, or long articles.
perverse: Someone perverse goes against what is right or sensible in a stubborn, twisted way. It is stronger than simply being unusual and often suggests bad judgement. It is easy to confuse with merely difficult, but difficulty alone does not make someone perverse.
pesky: Pesky means mildly annoying, especially because the trouble keeps coming back. It is playful and informal, so it suits small everyday problems better than serious criticism. A noisy neighbour or a broken tap can be pesky.
phenomenon: A phenomenon is a fact, event, or experience that people can notice and study. We often use it for something unusual or important, but it can also describe any observed situation. It is more common in science and formal writing than in casual talk.
phlegmatic: A phlegmatic person stays calm and shows little emotion, even when other people would react strongly. The word can sound positive, but it may also suggest that the person is too passive or slow to act. It is close to being unflappable.
phobia: A phobia is a very strong fear that continues over time and may cause real changes in behaviour. People sometimes use the word jokingly for an extreme dislike, such as fearing public speaking. Unlike dislike, a phobia can seriously affect daily life.
pick-of-the-crop: This refers to the best person or thing in a group. People use it to praise someone who stands out, such as the top student or finest product. The image comes from choosing the best fruit or vegetables after a harvest.
pick-on-someone-your-own-size: You are choosing an opponent who is as strong or important as you are. People use this when talking about fairness: do not attack or criticize someone weaker just because they are an easy target. The image is picking a fight with someone of the same size.
